Research presentations covered emerging model systems and sovereign AI, while livestreams broadened access to talks and interviews. The speaker lineup reflected a blend of government, academia, and industry perspectives, offering attendees rich, hands-on technical knowledge alongside policy insights.

Sponsors and ecosystem partners actively contributed through well-staffed booths, VIP dinners, hiring conversations, and hosting of partner rooms. Notable participants included Google DeepMind, OpenAI with Codex demos and workshops, Z.ai as a diamond sponsor, and companies like Exa, Arize, Vercel, Cloudflare, and Cursor. Their involvement brought industry resources, technical credibility, and career opportunities, weaving a commercial layer into the builder-focused conference.

The event drew a diverse community of builders including students, volunteers, organizers, hackers in the Ralphthon, and attendees enjoying side events and meetups. Posts celebrated student ticket access, partnerships with 65labs, warm community interactions, and active engagement in workshops and hackathons, reflecting grassroots energy and strong local builder infrastructure supporting the AI engineering movement.

Highlights of AI Engineer Singapore included Vivian Balakrishnan’s keynote revealing his second-brain AI agent, immersive technical workshops on LlamaIndex and agentic workflows, engaging Codex-based demos and interactions, research talks on advanced model systems, and creative stage demonstrations like Reachy robotics and rap battles. The event also featured vibrant side events, lively social gatherings, and accessible livestreams to extend the experience beyond the physical venue.

Brand presence was strong with active participation from global and regional AI leaders. OpenAI showcased Codex through workshops and booths; Google DeepMind had a prominent booth and networking dinners; Z.ai brought sessions highlighting Chinese open-weight models; and startups like Cursor and Simular presented demos and talks. The inclusion of brands from multiple geographies underscored Singapore’s strategic role as a builder hub converging Western and Eastern innovations.

posts.text: “You cannot govern a technology you’ve only been briefed on.” This morning, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan walked into a room full of builders and did something that genuinely mattered: …he showed up as one himself He opened up his actual workflow, talked through the second brain he’s been building, the tradeoffs, the implications, the limits, and the things he’s still figuring out. And I’m sure, before he spoke, there were skeptics in the room. Builders have heard enough people talk about technology from a distance to know the difference between someone who has touched the tools and someone who has only read summaries about them. What struck me most wasn’t even the talk itself, it was what happened after He stayed. He went off stage and spent time with young builders. Students. Engineers. People still figuring out their place in all of this. Then he stayed in the room to watch Gavriel Cohen’s creator of NanoClaw talk because he genuinely wanted to hear it. And as someone on the organising team, I can tell you that none of it was staged and all of it was him. That detail will stay with me for a long time. There were students sitting in the front row today who now have a completely different reference point for what leadership can look like. He wasn’t speaking above the work. He was actually doing it. I’m very aware that what happened today was much bigger than us. Thank you, Minister Vivian Balakrishnan. Putting together 65labs AI Engineer has always been rooted in a hope that Singapore can become a place where serious builders collide openly, generously, and ambitiously. posts.text:
Singapore’s Foreign Minister built his personal AI agent on a Raspberry Pi.

8GB of RAM. Hardware that’s two to three years old. Assembling open-source tools he found on GitHub. No code written.

He was doing this while managing the foreign affairs of a nation.

Dr Vivian Balakrishnan spoke at AI Engineer Singapore on 16 May. I’d watched videos of politicians talking about AI. This was different. He was talking as a builder.

His clearest line: “The barriers have fallen.”

Not just for engineers but for everyone. His argument: real value from AI isn’t created in data centres or government committees. It’s created workflow by workflow, individual by individual. The teacher who uses it to prepare better lessons. The lawyer who uses it to research faster. The diplomat who uses it to brief himself on 12 countries in a month.

He also said something I found very helpful: 
1. you can outsource computation. You cannot outsource understanding. 
2. You can delegate work. You cannot delegate accountability.

Viveka. That’s what he was describing. The Sanskrit term for discernment. The one human faculty that doesn’t get replaced. It gets amplified.

The speech is 22 minutes. Worth every minute.

posts.text:
I don’t think Singapore needs to become the next Silicon Valley for AI.
That was my biggest takeaway from Dr Vivian Balakrishnan speaking at AI Engineer Singapore.

In the US, AI is mostly pushed by founders, labs, venture capital, and a lot of chaos.
That works for them.
But Singapore is different.
We are not going to out-chaos San Francisco. And honestly, we probably should not try.
Our advantage is more boring, but maybe more useful: institutions, trust, governance, and the ability to roll things out properly.

The real question is not whether Singapore can build the next OpenAI.
It is whether we can become one of the best places in the world to turn AI from impressive demos into actual daily workflows.

Government workflows. Banking workflows. SME workflows. Healthcare workflows. Education workflows.
That is where the real productivity gain is.

My view is San Francisco will build many of the models.
Singapore’s opportunity is to show what serious adoption looks like.
The future of AI may be built in San Francisco.
But it could be tested, trusted, and deployed in Singapore.

posts.text:
ai engineer singapore just wrapped, and i still don’t think i’ve fully processed it - or recovered from the sleep deprivation.

this was a labor of love from our organizing team. 
i’m still sitting with everything that happened, but i wanted to share a few moments that stayed with me most.

speakers flying in from around the world - many of whom we’d only known through the internet - showing up for builders here in singapore. staying late after talks, talking to students, and genuinely wanting to help (some even sharing they're thinking of moving to singapore 👀 )

minister Vivian Balakrishnan showing what it looks like when a world leader doesn’t just get briefed on ai, but actually tinkers with the tools himself. 
that conversation alone has already sparked debate and reached millions online.

students realizing the infrastructure and access are already here - made possible by individual people who chose to sponsor scholars - to show up and care enough to support the next generation.

and across almost every session, the same thread kept emerging:
ai is forcing us to think more deeply about what it actually means to be human.

finally, the closing line hit me hard:
“you are the scene.”

i moved from silicon valley to singapore in 2018, and this place embraced me. over the past 8 years, i’ve seen how much talent exists here - often in ways that are quietly underestimated.

for a long time, it felt heartbreaking to hear people talk about singapore tech as if the only path forward was to leave - for founders to move abroad, for funds to pull out, for ambitious people to believe the real opportunities existed somewhere else.

this weekend reminded me how wrong that narrative is.

speakers, sponsors, founders, researchers, and engineers flew in from around the world because they believe something important is happening here. the scene is already here - and it was sitting in that room.

i see singapore as a forward-deployed nation - a place where frontier technology meets everyday people and companies faster than almost anywhere else in the world.

we tell people learning to vibe code that it only takes one step.
this weekend felt like a first step toward something much bigger.

more reflections soon. for now: grateful, overwhelmed, and already thinking about what comes next.

🥃 Agrim Singh  Nehal Agrawal Adlin Zainal  Ivan Leo Kaspar Hidayat Brian C. Daren T. 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan

posts.text: AI Engineer singapore starts tomorrow and i have some last minute thoughts it’s been a whirlwind 2 months pulling this together and i’m personally extremely proud of the weekend we’ve designed for all our attendees. we’ve been crystal clear about our aim with 65labs and our events - no bullshit. singapore deserves to respect itself as a technical hub with an overflow of talent that is underrepresented on the world stage. singapore deserves a quality of ai scene worthy of being globally rivaled. and we definitely have the capacities to make this happen in-house instead of flying 15 hours to find something reasonable. we also believe that technical-oriented events should not be locked to credentialed audiences and be accessible to people at large. for ai events, in particular, it is foolish to have grand events without builders at the centre of the discussion a this is how you entrench divide instead of empower newer audiences from coming on board. and we strongly believe that everyone is or can be a builder. so i sincerely hope that our attendees have a great time getting their hands dirty building and learning from folks we think are some of the sharpest minds in the industry. there are no glorified talks about ai safety or regulation - we want people to build, not be scared off. it won’t be perfect - it never is - but we strongly believe that by sunday evening folks who pass through AIE sg will have learned a whole bunch of new things, built with tech and met some cool companies and staff who, up till this point, have never set foot in singapore. let’s fkin get it. Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Adlin Zainal Kaspar Hidayat Ivan Leo Gabriel Chua Brian C. Daren T. Nehal Agrawal 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan (pic: war room at our house lol) So glad to be apart of this and help support the work y'all have put in! Love the energy and vibe you guys have been bringing throughout 🥃 Agrim Singh and team! Singapore is and has major worldwide respect as a dev hub, next to SF as a talent nucleus. Luma proves this. So grateful ❤️ Looking forward to seeing you all at SMU tomorrow and then Capitol! This is epic! Great energy, gonna be an awesome event 🎉 Same here, 2 months of no sleep! Not at the same scale as what you all are putting together but agree with you, Singapore deserves better because we are better than that! We have so much talent, personally I found that 2 years NS created a chip on the shoulder that every (male) graduate I hired was HUNGRY! For the ladies, well.... all you have to do is look at Rachael De Foe! GO SMASH IT YOU'ALL!

posts.text:
Just got back from an incredible 39 hours in Singapore!

🇸🇬 Had the honor of meeting with Singapore's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan to discuss the future of secure and democratized access to AI agents. Singapore's vision for responsible AI adoption is inspiring, and I'm grateful for the opportunity to be part of that conversation.

🎤 Followed the minister on stage at AI Engineer Singapore, where I spoke to 600+ AI engineers about the agent factory we built to review and test every pull request on NanoClaw, and how we do it securely.

🤖 To prove the security works, I invited the entire audience to chat with my personal agent. It's connected to my emails, calendar, and call notes. 300 people took me up on it. 12 booked coffee meetings with me through the agent, each one approved by me in real time.

🎙️ Recorded a podcast episode with Latent Space Podcast

Singapore blew me away. The energy, the talent, the ambition. First time visiting and I already know I'll be back.

Grateful to Sherry Jiang and the AI Engineer team for an incredible event, and to the Singapore tech community for the warm welcome.

Big news coming very soon. Stay tuned.

I’ve been on the road for a few days now, 8 AM to 8 PM every single day—weekdays and weekends alike. Meeting almost 1,000+ builders, founders, and “AI-curious” enthusiasts, having deep conversations, vibe coding, and soaking in everyone's ideas and perspectives. Every single chat left me inspired. It’s a unique moment in history because AI is no longer just for engineers. It is going to have a profound effect on designers, product managers, founders, and yes, even politicians. One thought from JJ’s talk really stuck with me: “The models are amazing!!! But also never good enough.” Think about the sheer progress humanity has made since the 2016 AlphaGo moment. Now, just imagine what the world will look like by 2036. 🚀 The Google booth was easily one of my highlights of the conference. We had a blast helping folks build on the spot with AI Studio! We also loved hosting so many incredible founders who joined us for the Google for Startups x Google DeepMind happy hour. 🥂 Special thanks to my partners in crime this week: Zhi Yi Ho Ivan Leo Thu Ya K. Nicole Yap Janti Tang alongside our incredible Google Developer Group leads, Google Developer Experts, Googlers and other volunteers. And a massive shout-out to the team at 65labs — Sherry 🥃 Agrim Adlin Rachael Kaspar — for kickstarting a massive new movement in Singapore and across Southeast Asia. I’ve seen people think, build, and ship ideas in under 15 minutes through vibe coding via AI Studio and Antigravity. When else in history has this been possible? And this is just the start. posts.text: No funding. No government mandate. No strategy deck. Just borrowed rooms, called-in favours, and a belief that Singapore's AI builders needed somewhere to collide. That's how 65labs started. Today, it's Singapore's largest grassroots AI builder community at 5,000 members strong, and it has outgrown every single venue it has ever been given. There's a lesson in that. e27's coverage here: https://lnkd.in/g24S2YtV The gap was never talent. Singapore has always had talented people. The gap was what Sherry Jiang, 65labs co-founder, calls "the invisible machinery": the third spaces, the casual collisions, the culture of showing up for each other without an agenda. The infrastructure that Silicon Valley built over decades and that most ecosystems are still trying to replicate. 65labs didn't wait for permission to build it. What I find genuinely interesting about this community is the deliberate standard they set early: if you take the stage, you show something you actually built. No panels. No speculation. No keynotes from people who aren't close to the work. That one decision filtered the room naturally. The people who come to be seen stopped coming. The people who come to build kept coming back. The result? OpenAI chose 65labs to run its first official Codex hackathon in Singapore. Cursor held its first Singapore event through the community. And this weekend, 65labs is hosting AI Engineer World's Fair, the world's leading conference for AI engineers, for its first-ever Asia stop. All of this from a weekend project run by founders with full-time jobs elsewhere. The parallel that comes to mind is the Homebrew Computer Club, a garage gathering where Steve Wozniak first showed up and went home to design what became the Apple I. The club never had more than a few hundred members. Its cultural legacy is incalculable. You don't always need scale to matter. You need the right room, the right standard, and the discipline to protect both as you grow. The co-founders of 65labs have a simple metric they keep returning to: are the people who showed up before anyone was watching still in the room? That's a question every ecosystem builder should be asking. Keep the builders building! 🥃 Agrim Singh Sherry Jiang Will you be there at AIE? Hope to catch you over the weekend Mohan Belani 🏃♂️ just doing what good people back in the day did for me 🫡 Best example of a new community that's grown with a strong vision! yeah, agree. very impressive, well deserved success. ty for building the community, Sherry Jiang and 🥃 Agrim Singh 🙏 Strong example of how culture and standards, not scale or funding, can shape a real builder ecosystem. Mohan Belani 🏃♂️ Anisa Menur A. Maulani thank you for always taking the time to hear out stories from the community! e27 does a great job amplifying the community! I've met the team, they are AMAZING Thanks for cropping the picture just nice that I'm barely at the corner of it Anisa Menur A. Maulani! Super proud of these boys 🥃 Agrim Singh and the entire crew 65labs! keep going guys True. It proves the famous phrase "If you build it, they will come"!

posts.text: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan walked into AI Engineer Singapore today and said the quiet part out loud: "You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on." A Foreign Minister who has actually built with the tools. Who knows context windows are the budget. Who knows the model is the commodity and the wiring is the product. Who knows stateless chat is a dead end for real work. That is what learning by doing looks like at the top. And it's a quiet indictment of every AI conversation happening in a boardroom right now where nobody in the room has actually shipped anything. The executive summary tells you what the tech does. Building with it tells you where it breaks, what it costs, and what it still can't do. There is no shortcut around that — not a consultancy deck, not a workshop, not a steering committee. Three messages from his talk worth pinning to the wall: → You can outsource memory and computation. You cannot outsource understanding → Real value shows up when the people who understand the work: teachers, doctors, engineers, even ministers get tools that re-engineer how they do it → The barriers to access ane value have just collapsed So less talking about talking. More building. The minister did the homework. What’s our excuse? Our move. Gives us all a good kick. Reminds me of the cooking show "If Yan Can Cook, So Can You". All of us need to understand how AI can re-engineer what we do and allow us to solve more complex problems. Already, in cybersecurity, the speed of vulnerability discovery has challenged us to think about how we should deliver software. One site that encapsulates this point neatly is https://zerodayclock.com/. The "Call to Action" is meaningful to read also. Strong message 👍 That line really hits ,understanding only comes when you actually build and break things yourself, not just read about them. AI especially exposes this gap between “knowing” and “doing.” Real clarity comes only after hands-on work I took of a photo of that very slide. I think it’s also true of business decision makers. Which Singapore agency would you want Dr Vivian to actually code in next?

posts.text: Attended AI Engineer Singapore leadership track yesterday. Sharing some learnings: 1. Don't just add AI tools, fix the workflow first. Adopting AI tools (Copilot, Jira AI, etc.) won't move the needle if approvals still happen over email, requirements live in PDFs, and decisions are tribal knowledge. Remove workflow waste before layering on AI. 2. Engineer roles are shifting from doers to managers. Teams are shrinking and becoming "fleet managers" overseeing AI agents rather than writing code themselves. Expect more code review, spec writing, and parallel task management, less heads-down individual coding. 3. Spec writing becomes a core skill. AI agents are only as good as the instructions they receive. Invest in training people to write clear, structured specs and acceptance criteria. This is now a high-leverage activity. This should apply to all kinds of documentation. 4. Measure outcomes, not activity. Don't track lines of code or token consumption. Track passing test cases, delivery speed, and problems solved. Productivity gains must translate to business outcomes. 5. Leadership must send a clear signal Executives need to visibly commit, not just provide tools, but drive cultural change. People sitting on the fence need to be pushed. Hire and reward people who use AI to raise their own output. 6. Governance and security can't be an afterthought. Private data access, exposure to untrusted content, and external communication channels create real risk. Build guardrails, rules, and hooks into the AI workflow from the start. Thank you Sherry Jiang Tomas Laboutka and the rest of the team for organizing this event. #ai #leadership #management Hi Shawn, thanks for the insight. Curious if you have pointers for the trainings that you think will be most effective for point 3?

posts.text:
I spent the last few days at AI Engineer Singapore 2026 after flying in from Tokyo, and the experience was really great so I would like to share my experience. For starters, the conference kicked off with Singapore’s Minister of Foreign Affairs talking about his own experience tinkering with LLMs, including building a personal “second brain” using NanoClaw. He mentioned that you cannot govern what you do not understand, which was a very interesting way to open the event, especially because the rest of the conference also had this strong feeling of people trying to understand AI by building with it directly. There were many talks and workshops, but a few themes stood out to me: 1) Software factories: I joined talks and workshops by Cursor, OpenAI, Stripe’s Minions, and other agentic engineering workflows. What I found interesting was that a lot of the discussion was not only about making coding agents smarter, but about the system around them such as dev environments, review loops, Slack interfaces, and deterministic hooks. 2. More "human" AI: Talks from Blue Labs, ego AI (YC W24), OpenMind, and others made this direction feel less abstract to me. The focus was not only better task completion, but also memory, personality, trust, and the relationship between humans and AI systems. 3. Design and taste: I do not have a strong background here but I appreciated seeing design treated as a core part of building useful AI products, not just as polish at the end. My biggest takeaway is that when people talk about the AI frontier, the conversation often defaults to model intelligence. That is still important, of course, but the road to actually useful AI seems to have many other frontiers too: agent orchestration and software factories, evals, product experience, trust, and making these systems feel natural to work with. There are many frontiers to work on, so it is an exciting time to be in this field. I also left with a strong impression of Singapore as an AI hub, and it feels like things here are only getting started. Thank you to the organizers (🥃 Agrim Singh Sherry Jiang and others), speakers, and all the amazing people I got to meet. I’m really glad I made the trip and I hope I can attend similar events in the future.

Amazing insight! Thanks for sharing! 🔥 I'm interested to learn more about software factories now, sounds like a future of software development

posts.text:
"YOU ARE THE SCENE" 🇸🇬 

This weekend wasn't about a conference. It was about people looking around and realising they weren't building alone.

For a long time, Singapore's builder scene didn't always know how much it was worth because it hadn't fully seen itself yet:
All the late-night hacks, small meetups, group chats, parents trying tools after work, students learning from open tabs and Discord threads, our Foreign Minister himself building a "second brain" with open-source tools. 

...Basically builders trying to find their people.

Then, for 3 days, everyone could actually see each other. And the frontier of AI flew down to meet them too. All at once.

That matters ❤️‍🔥

A few packed rooms won't birth an ecosystem. But seeing everyone around you building does. It changes what you believe is possible and let's you know it can happen right here.

What moved a bunch of us to tears (or maybe me at the very least haha) wasn't the scale, or the logos, or the sold-out rooms.

It was builders being there for each other. Whether they were on stage or on the conference floor, sharing how they're building because they wanted to bring others into the fold too.

AI should never feel distant from the work. The future should be shaped by people close enough to build it, question it, break it, and make it better.

Singapore is SO much earlier in its story than people realise.

Sherry Jiang 🥃 Agrim Singh Nehal Agrawal Adlin Zainal Ivan Leo Kaspar Hidayat Brian C. Daren T. 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan AI Engineer

posts.text:
Today at ai.engineer Singapore, it didn’t feel like a tech demo, it felt like a glimpse of a future where AI helps more people participate in creativity, work, and self-expression ...not fewer. We gave a talk about Synthaesthetic Art, brain-computer interfaces, shared autonomy, and the path that led us to a live robotic painting demonstration controlled through brain activity. A few years ago, this all started as an idea between myself and Dr Richard Savery. At the time, we were exploring a much broader question around AI and creativity: "What happens when humans and intelligent systems stop being separate roles, and instead become collaborators inside the same creative process?" That became the foundation for what we now call Synthaesthetic Art, it's a form of human-machine creative collaboration combining AI systems, robotics, generative models, physical embodiment, and human expression into a shared creative loop. Back then it was mostly experimental prototypes, hacked together systems, robotic painting rigs, generative pipelines, OSC messages flying everywhere, and lots of discussions about whether AI could amplify creativity instead of flattening it. Today felt like one of those moments where the original vision suddenly becomes very real. On stage, Kai Ming N., who is living with EDS, participated in a live painting session using our shared autonomy system. Her brain activity became the control system driving a robotic painting process combining AI, robotics, generative systems, and human intent. And honestly, it was emotional. Not because of the tech, but because it felt like watching Kai Ming reconnect with a form of expression that had been partially taken away from her. That’s the part I keep thinking about tonight: there’s so much conversation right now about AI replacing humans, removing people from workflows what we experienced today pointed in the opposite direction! AI as amplification, as restoration, as a pathway back to participation. The idea of shared autonomy has become increasingly important to me over the last few years: systems where humans and machines compensate for each other’s limitations rather than competing against each other. This has implications far beyond art. Huge thank you to the team: Dr Richard Savery who has been working on this with me from the original concept all the way through to what happened on stage today. Ivy Chen whose artistic vision and experimentation helped shape the direction of Synthaesthetic Art itself. Jackie Tan for helping make a complicated live system function under conference demo conditions, always the most dangerous possible environment for robotics and AI demos! And most importantly, thank you Kai Ming N.. What you shared with the audience today took courage, vulnerability, and trust. Today genuinely didn’t feel like a technology demo. It felt like a glimpse of a future where AI helps more people participate in creativity, work, and self-expression.

Our robotic father is fathering. 🤩 AI Engineer is never just about "AI" and "Engineering" but about human, how we connect better, imagine bigger and achieve what we cannot achieve in the past. Thank you team for expressing Tech with courage, vulnerability and trust. .....and that itself is a real art.

Technology matters less than helping people rediscover creative abilities they believed were gone. RAI AI demonstrates where artificial intelligence should head by delivering genuinely personalized insights tailored to individual needs instead of producing one-size-fits-all results.

this was absolutely incredible - and was extremely moving to hear kai ming n's story. there is so much that ai could do to create opportunity, and loved hearing that uplifting message.

this is awesome, Justin :)

Big congratulations I would like to explore opportunities to bring AI Engineer to Africa 🌍

Beautiful moment!

posts.text:
Singapore's Foreign Minister keynoted an AI engineering conference. Then demoed an AI assistant he built himself. On a Raspberry Pi.

That was Saturday morning at AI Engineer Singapore 2026 — and it set the tone for the entire weekend.

Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan walked through "A Second Brain for a Diplomat" — assembled with Claude Agent SDK, mnemon graph, Ollama, and whisper.cpp. Running on a Pi 5. His own code, his own assembly.

When a sitting Foreign Minister is shipping his own agent stack, the debate is over. The question now is how fast everyone else catches up.

Three days at SMU. Frontier ideas, generous people, and a community that genuinely felt like San Francisco in the heart of Southeast Asia. Still buzzing as I write this.

A few takeaways worth your time:

→ Engineers are becoming "fleet managers" of agents. Verification — not generation — is the real bottleneck now.

→ Frontier firms aren't bolting AI on top. They're redesigning workflows end-to-end. Executive buy-in plus broad team access is the moat. (OpenAI)

→ Open weights are a strategic choice — for security, sovereignty, and ecosystem control. Boards should be paying attention. (Z.ai)

And three quotes I'm still chewing on:

"If you haven't had your 'oh f***' moment after two years, you're behind." — Geoff Huntley

"Token consumption is a mindset for harder problems, not a vanity metric." — Z.ai

"We extract institutional context the same way the FBI does — lock them in a room. Then we rebuild from scratch anyway." — Jeff, Belli

🙏 Massive credit to swyx, Sherry Jiang, grim, Rachael, Vishay, Tomas Laboutka, and the entire 65Labs team for pulling this off through Friday's monsoon — and to John Allsopp for the cross-event camaraderie from AI Engineer Melbourne. The warmth, the hawker tours, and the flawless logistics did not go unnoticed.

The Lion City is officially on the AI engineering map.

For leaders in Telco, IT, and global business - Curious to know how India Bangladesh or South East Asia, Nigeria-Kenya or Africa -based teams are thinking about this. When a sitting Foreign Minister is shipping AI on a Pi, where is your organisation on the curve? Still piloting on the side, or actively redesigning how work gets done? Always keen in learning from your view.

#AIEngineer #AIESG2026 #Singapore #AILeadership #Gratitude

posts.text:
Don't want to dunk on Singapore, but with the AI Engineer conference being in town, my timeline is flooded with delusional takes. The reality is that Singapore is mostly a trading hub. It's incredibly well-run, tax-friendly and great for young families. But it isn't some sort of technological utopia. The density of talent, ambition, and success is nowhere near what you would find in SF, NYC, London or Beijing. "But it's a massive market for Nvidia and Claude!". It's a pass-through for China. How do you think they got their hands on AI chips? How do you think they distill models from OpenAI and Anthropic? "But what about Manus?". You mean the Chinese company? Whose founders are currently barred from leaving Beijing? For tech companies, Singapore is mostly a sales office for APAC. They may have some FDEs and devrels, but they don't do serious product or research work here.

A country of ~6M people ranking #2 globally in per-capita Claude usage is quite telling. 😉

true at present but defeatist, this is the same as many who think singapore can never do better than labor arbitrage - i'm ultra bullish on young smart ambitious people, we do produce many, and the times they are changing

Punching above its per capita weight easily

The problem is structural - Singapore is a city-state. There's no other city you can move to to reinvent yourself. In the US, you can fail in NYC and start over in SF. Literally do it over & over again. In Singapore, that's not possible. So locals don't take chances. There's a risk of Failure becoming more of an identity when you're around the same neighbourhoods you grew up in as a kid and taking chances. Also, doesn't help that ASEAN is 6 different markets with 6 different complexities for a disproportional upside. In comparison, 1000 KM radius around the city of SF has more in GDP than the entirety of ASEAN. But I certainly see things changing rapidly in terms of the culture. More of my generation getting off the traditional "safe" paths and taking chances. Singapore's greatest weakness is also it's greatest strength - If it wants to move in a certain direction, it can do so faster than most cities because of it's size and management.

I love the confidence of this take paired with the "I have no idea what I'm doing" tagline. It sets up an interesting ambiguity for me as a reader

Biggest problem is the customers. Unless you are very niche, Asian customers will prefer buying bigger brands. Also, if most of your early customers are in the US (both consumer and B2B), unless you want to take calls and deal with issues at wee hours, then it makes more sense to build from the US. The customers are the root of the ecosystem, theres no way to sustain an ecosystem without constant cash flow.

Wouldn't be the first time in history that someone underestimated Singapore's abilities 🙂↔️

Attention leads money. It might not be comparable now, but tech moves fast and opportunities come to societies which embrace these changes structurally.

Yeah to a large extent... the talent pipeline is not encouraged to run startups or develop "serious" research. That's why we have so many educated financial advisers and real estate agents in one of the most highly educated per capita countries in the world.

posts.text: Just wrapped up an unforgettable experience at the first ever AI Engineer Singapore! 🇸🇬 The absolute highlight of the event wasn't just meeting the amazing community and the incredible tech on display, but getting to share it all with my son, Usman. Introducing him to physical AI, seeing his excitement checking out the humanoid robots, and exploring the community together made it a truly special trip. A massive personal highlight was catching up with Nigel Cheong. Nigel is an absolute powerhouse! an AI Engineer by week (shoutout to his journey through the Google SG trainee program) and a MasterChef over the weekend! Good to see you Nigel and Keep Rocking!. The event kicked off with a phenomenal keynote from Minister for Foreign Affairs Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan (who literally "vibe coded" his own AI assistant on a Raspberry Pi Stack), followed by deep technical deep-dives into what it actually takes Agents from Prototyping to Production (Agent Harness, tools, registries, context management, and guardrails). Here are the biggest takeaways that stuck with me from the sessions: You Cannot Outsource Understanding. You can outsource memory and computation, but true governance requires building. Reading an executive summary tells you what tech does; actually building with it tells you where it breaks, what it costs, and hence learning by doing is paramount. The real value is in re-engineering workflows. The massive economic and societal shifts won’t just come from tech giants—the Tech is aavailable, they happen when everyday professionals (bankers, doctors, lawyers, teachers, and yes, ministers!) use AI to completely redesign how they get the job done and enterprises follow the suit. The barriers to entry have collapsed. The tools are here. It's no longer about who has the biggest R&D budget; it's about who has the curiosity to assemble these tools and put them to work. From Builders to Artists (AI as a Magic Pencil). As the barriers to entry collapse, the distinction between roles—engineers, PMs, designers, founders—is blurring. AI is a "magic pencil." Follow the curiosity and use these tools to completely re-engineer workflows and deliver Value. From talking about agentic frameworks to workshops, to watching Usman point out humanoid robots on stage, the energy here proves that Singapore is a true center for practical, curious AI builders. Time to head home, stay curious, and keep tinkering! ✨ #AIEngineersg #AIgovernence #AISingapore #GenerativeAI #AgenticAI #TechInnovation #Parenting #NextGenBuilders #Robotics #Google #Deepmind #Leadership #Gemini #AugmentedAI #prototypingtoproduction #GTMEngineer * +3

posts.text: Over the weekend, I had the opportunity to participate in the AI Engineer Hackathon, hosted by the 65labs team as part of the road to AI Engineer 🇸🇬 Conference. The event was a 7-hour open-canvas build day with hundreds of builders experimenting, prototyping, and pushing AI tools as far as we could. I decided to build a game: Prompt Bound Prompt Bound is a retro pixel side-scroller that teaches AI engineering through play. Instead of explaining concepts in slides, the game turns them into levels: prompting, context, retrieval, tool calling, and agents. Players move through each trial, meet characters, solve agent-themed challenges, collect rewards, and gradually learn how to work with AI Agents more thoughtfully. I built this because AI engineering can feel abstract when you first encounter it. A game gave me a way to make the learning loop more immediate. The 65labs team consistently create excellent spaces for builders to meet, learn, and ship things together, and this hackathon was no exception. And huge congrats to the finalists and winners! Your pitches were amazing 🤩 Prompt Bound is not live yet; more improvements need to be made 😊 AI Engineer Singapore is sold out, but you can still join the community around it: explore AI Engineer Singapore side events here: https://lnkd.in/gDjyJgKF Learn more about the main conference here: https://lnkd.in/g4Vs5UrU also shoutout to Codex! posts.text: Day 1 at AI Engineer Singapore! Today was filled with workshops, and it was such an experience! I attended sessions by Exa (led by conrad soon), Convex (led by Michael Cann), Resaro (led by Timothy Lin), and Arize AI (led by Sean Lee and Fuad A.) which covered various topics across web search for AI, reliable AI app backends, scenario-specific benchmarks and evaluation, and production agent workflows. There were so many other interesting workshops happening in parallel that I would have loved to attend too, but unfortunately I could only be in one place at a time :) A few takeaways from today: 1. Search for AI is very different from search for humans, not only in terms of the output format, but also latency, relevance and diversity. 2. Building reliable AI apps goes beyond just the model. The backend, data flow, structured queries, state management, and how the system handles failures matter a lot. 3. Broad benchmarks are useful but not enough. As such, these benchmarks and evaluations must be tied to a specific use case. Here, I really liked the framing around operational design domains, golden datasets, and test cases that reflect the conditions the system is actually meant to work in. 4. Many things can break in production - prompts, models, user behaviours etc. This makes tracing, evals, iteration, and feedback loops essential for building systems. 5. Conversations are a really big part of events like these. As a student, I learnt a lot not just from the workshop content, but also from the questions people asked and the way senior developers, researchers, founders, product builders, and engineers thought about real-world AI systems. I also got to meet some of the other students from the student cohort - Jesmine Goh, Cheng Ye, K Jagateesvaran, Wilson Soon and Lucius Chee. It was really nice being around peers who are also curious about AI, research, and building real-world systems. Special thanks to Max Buckley from Exa, with whom we had a really insightful conversation about retrieval, research and much more! Excited for the next two days and to meet more people building in this space. If you’re at AI Engineer Singapore this weekend, I would love to meet! Great to meet you! Had a very interesting conversation with u! You are a bright girl! Keep building n hustling! This is so awesome ! Its great to see Students from around the world gathering and getting connected for AI :). Stay blessed !

posts.text: Day 2 at AI Engineer Singapore! Today was honestly super packed (but in a good way!) with so many talks, conversations and booths, that it is difficult to capture everything in one post. The day started with the honour of hearing from Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, about how he built his “second brain.” We got to sit in the front row and take a photo together, which was a really special start to the day. Some highlights from the rest of the day: > I got to hear Gavriel Cohen, founder of NanoClaw, during his talk, and later had a coffee chat with him. We mainly talked about security, and he gave very insightful tips to someone like me who is just starting out. > I attended a virtual talk by Thibault Sottiaux from the OpenAI Codex team on coding agents and where Codex and coding agents may be heading. > I was personally very excited for Daria Soboleva’s talk (Cerebras), especially after having read about her work on mixture-of-experts models. It was really cool to connect something I had studied academically with the way these ideas show up in AI systems and research today. posts.text:
Last week at AI Engineer Singapore, our research scientist Stefania Druga presented Sakana AI's view of Sovereign AI.
(YouTube: https://lnkd.in/dZJP9FD4)

Sovereign AI is often described as "every country building its own foundation model." We see it more broadly: as the ability to take in the world's best models while shaping their behavior to local culture, institutions, and safety needs, and remaining accountable for AI's role in society. Sovereignty is built from layers (data, model adaptation, coordination across models, governance), and each country chooses which to own and which to share with the world. That pattern of choices is what sovereignty looks like in practice.

Stefania mapped this thinking onto four of our projects: Sakana Chat / Namazu, which adapts open frontier models to Japan; The AI Scientist, which automates the research process itself; Sakana Fugu, which coordinates multiple models so the ensemble outperforms any single one; and CTM, a brain-inspired alternative to the transformer.

She also covered our institutional work in Japan. With megabanks like MUFG and SMBC Group, more than a thousand pieces of expert feedback flow back into our credit memo workflows, turning tacit, never-digitized know-how into something a model can actually learn. With the Japanese government, our team has shown how AI-driven intelligence, drawing on social media analysis, can trace how misinformation campaigns originate and spread. These are domains where data, workflows, and accountability all need to stay close to home, and where Sovereign AI is put to its most practical test.

She closed with her own message: from kids to parents to researchers to AI engineers, we all have agency, and local agency matters more than global capability.

Huge thanks to AI Engineer and the vibrant community there for having us.

posts.text: I cleared my weekend to attend the most coveted AI conference in Singapore. My eczema had other plans. Day 1 of AI Engineer Singapore had me buzzing with ideas as I moved within SMU for workshops I secured weeks in advance. I pushed through in Singapore humidity to learn from the builders actively shipping in this space. I even arranged conversations with speakers I wanted to go deeper with. I unfortunately ended Day 1 with a full-body eczema flare once I returned to my hotel room (which I booked to be much nearer to the event venues). I made the painful decision to “miss” attending Day 2 in person. Fortunately, AI Engineer Singapore had made the main stage talks freely available — a ten-hour livestream, no paywall. So I watched from bed, hours after they aired. But then I started catching up on the LinkedIn notifications I had missed. Students chosen to attend the conference on scholarship tickets were posting their delighted reflections. All of them tagged their sponsors by name, unprompted by the organisers. One of the names was mine. I hadn’t announced it on any platform yet, but I was a personal contributor to the student scholarships when organiser Rachael De Foe shared an invitation to do so. Having been a university student who benefited from scholarships and bursaries, I had seen a chance to give back. Reading the students’ posts had me feeling more present in the room than I was attending the workshops in person on Day 1. Being absent from the room made me realise I’d never fully appreciated what the room was actually for. It’s not just livestreams and recordings that make the AI conversation accessible. It’s the networking and inspiration that happens out of being in the same physical space. The offhand introduction that turns into mentorship and even business opportunities. The ambient credibility of having been there, among the people actively shaping where AI goes next in this region, not merely learning from them. I’m talking about social capital, not just skills and experience. We talk about making AI accessible. We usually mean free tools, open-source models, public livestreams. But accessibility is also: who gets to be in the rooms where relationships are made. Who gets introduced to whom. Who gets the warm referral that opens the next door. The students who tagged me didn’t need my contribution to be capable. They needed one barrier removed so everything they already had could compound. I wasn’t in the room on Day 2. But I was still in the room — because I’d helped put someone else there first. If you’re in a position to do the same — a scholarship, a referral, an open calendar, even a workshop — you don’t have to wait for a formal programme. Build access intentionally. The way you’d design any system worth building. 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang, Kaspar Hidayat, Nehal Agrawal, Gabriel Chua * +1 A powerful reflection on how true accessibility in AI goes beyond content and tools, and extends to the relationships and opportunities created when we help others get into the room. this is incredibly inspiring, the way you created access for others :) speedy recovery! glad we got to chat! :D So inspiring Ainul! Thank you for all that you do and I’ve so much to learn from you. you are a legend. hope u feel better soon!! Hope you get well soon, I'll be replying your questions shortly! That's really kind of you! Hope you're recovering well ain, we missed you yesterday! thank you again for being so generous and thoughtful about why you wanted to give. once this is over, let’s do a meetup, i know the students would love to meet. :)

posts.text:
"We are perhaps one of the most privileged generations to be living through a revolution."

That's how Singapore's Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan closed his keynote at AIE Singapore where he shared how he built a personal AI agent on NanoClaw and what he's learned from it.

He calls his NanoClaw agent his "second brain for a diplomat", saying he doesn't dare turn it off. 

Why NanoClaw? He picked it for the security, the readable codebase, and the containerized architecture. 

He said it himself, "As a surgeon, I know things will go wrong. When they break, you want them to break within barriers." 

He talks to it through WhatsApp, and, on top of it all, there are no config files to wrestle with. The agent relies on the LLM itself to handle all the customization, which means every person running NanoClaw is essentially running their own bespoke system.

So what does he use it for? The use-cases seem endless: briefings on the 12 countries he's visiting this month, remembering the hundreds of people he meets along the way, and first drafts of speeches and parliamentary answers.

And with that, his three rules for AI:

1. You can outsource computation, memory, and dissemination. You cannot outsource personal understanding. And if you hold authority, you cannot delegate accountability.

2. The real value AI brings society won't come from frontier labs. It'll come when people who actually know their jobs (teachers, technicians, doctors, lawyers, even ministers) embrace AI and rebuild how they do the work.

3. The barriers to building this have collapsed. Anyone can assemble these tools today, but you must get your hands dirty and learn by doing.

Sure, frontier models grab the headlines, but the real future gets built one workflow at a time, by people who actually know their craft. And, today, getting started has never been more accessible.

We couldn't be prouder to be part of this revolution, and to power your second brain, Minister!

Check out Dr. Balakrishnan's full speech — linked in comments!

posts.text: REACHY RAP BATTLE SHOWDOWN - AI.ENGINEER SINGAPORE Unveiled at ai.engineer in Singapore today (Thorsten Schaeff as promised 🤣) Hugging Face Pollen Robotics Reachy rap battle, powered by Google DeepMind, ElevenLabs and more... Along with my long time collaborator Dr Richard Savery we built a real-time AI rap battle system with two Reachy Mini robots. (1) The flow: A human drops a prompt spoken on the mic. Local speech-to-text transcribes the prompt on an Apple Silicon Mac using MLX Whisper. The text is sent to Gemini, which writes alternating rap battle verses for two characters. Each battle verse is rendered with custom ElevenLabs voices. The system combines the voices into a stereo battle track, with one rapper on the left channel and the other on the right. At the same time, we generate a timing manifest that maps each rap turn to a specific robot animation. Cycling '74 Max/MSP handles playback and show control. Python handles AI generation, voice rendering, timing, OSC messages, and robot choreography. The two Reachy Mini robots connect over WiFi and USB. When the battle plays, each robot performs when its voice is rapping, while the other keeps a smaller beat-driven groove so both stay alive on stage. The robots’ movement is word-aware: emphasized words create stronger gestures, and each robot has its own animation personality. The system prewarms robot connections before playback so audio and motion start in sync. (2) the Stack: Max/MSP, Python, Gemini, ElevenLabs, MLX Whisper, OSC, Reachy Mini SDK, Apple Silicon. A small fun idea turned into a full AI performance pipeline: prompt in, rap battle out, two robots arguing on beat 😎 And as mentioned in the video, special thanks to 🥃 Agrim Singh and Sherry Jiang and the whole 65labs team for making ai.engineer Singapore happen, and for listening to my crazy ideas about setting up a Robot Playground for the Embodied AI track! The video was on. The notes were a mess. I couldn't return to what I'd learned at AIE Singapore Day 1 without re-watching the whole thing — that's a tooling problem, not a memory one.

✅ Almost every operator named the same durable surface — orchestration. Skills, MCP, sandboxes, evals, playbooks. When a Singapore foreign minister, OpenAI, Stripe, Cursor, GovTech, and a Tokyo sovereign-AI lab all describe the same architecture in one day, the bet is no longer contrarian.

✅ World models, voice, real-time inference, robotics — the stack diverged on modality and consolidated on the orchestration layer. Same day.

posts.text:
Singapore’s AI workforce direction showed up in the last place I expected: our Foreign Minister’s personal agent for diplomatic work.

Dr Vivian Balakrishnan opened AI Engineer Singapore with the 8GB Raspberry Pi running his 'second brain' on NanoClaw.

His hands-on approach to enhance productivity was a microcosm of Singapore's AI direction.

Across 1,000+ builders and 91 speakers, the clearest thread I saw was this:

AI is moving from model access to the operating discipline of deploying agents at scale.

GovTech Singapore’s sovereign agentic harness made that hard to ignore: MCP gateway, versioned skills, identity, memory and observability, built for 150,000 public officers.

Harness architecture for a NATIONAL workforce.

Not “everyone gets a chatbot,” but an operating layer for human-agent collaboration.

Dr Vivian captured the shift: “Tools matter more than models.”

"Best model” is already an outdated frame. And Tejas Kumar broke it down succinctly:

Harnesses are what make or break the system because they serve as the control surface around black-box vendor models you can't otherwise trust.

Tool registry. Model selection. Context management. Guardrails. Agent loops. Verify steps.

JJ Geewax put the production principle cleanly:

“Surround the non-deterministic model with deterministic boundaries.”

Gavriel Cohen, founder of NanoClaw, made the security logic concrete with this analogy:

Agents operate behind enemy lines.

The agent isn't trusted by default. Credentials stay outside it, tool calls are separated from execution and privileged actions go through a vault/ broker, with approval.

NanoClaw hitting 30k stars and 12k forks in 3 months makes sense when you see what developers are really forking: 

A safer way to let agents work.

I spoke to Gavriel because I wanted to migrate my OpenClaw setup. His philosophy matched what I had been learning the expensive way.

But instead of pitching a migration, he suggested a spike test:

Let a NanoClaw agent extract key insights in cooperation with my existing OpenClaw agent. Then decide what tool surface my agents should own in my company.

This approach aligned with my vision for Maibel.

I’m building an AI-native startup around human-agent collaboration:

People for judgment, agents for bounded execution, shared memory for context, evals for quality, permissions for safety.

The future human-agent workforce won't be one omniscient agent plugged into everything.

It'll consist of different agents with different boundaries, permissions and tool surfaces, working inside an inspectable operating layer.

Right now, I run a tiny team of two humans and two agents. That constraint forces clarity.

Singapore might not build the best models. But we may win by getting unusually good at deployment.

Models matter. But weak harnesses turn intelligence into expensive chaos.

Dr Vivian’s 8GB Raspberry Pi made the metaphor obvious:

Lean machine. Serious operating discipline. 
That's our real AI advantage.

A full-time minister, a former eye surgeon, not a "technical" operator - yet deeply thoughtful about AI. It just made the whole space feel more accessible. Sharing some of my key insights yesterday: - Documentation isn't for humans anymore, it's for AI. Every outdated doc becomes a confident wrong answer at scale. - Efficiency is the wrong metric for personal decisions. The best AI doesn't decide faster. It helps you feel like the decision is yours. - Agent compromise isn't a possibility, it's a given. Stop chasing perfect agents. Start building better sandboxes. - AI made individuals 10x faster. Making teams 10x faster? Still unsolved. When execution gets cheap, alignment becomes the bottleneck. - Great design isn't pixels. It's psychology. That's still deeply human. Excited for the rest of the sessions, so many more interesting nuggets already! (Sharing the YT livestream for both day 1 recap and day 2 in the comments if you want in!)

posts.text:
Singapore’s Foreign Minister just published the architecture of his personal AI assistant. It runs on a Raspberry Pi on his desk. He says he doesn’t dare switch it off.

Vivian Balakrishnan’s “second brain” ingests his WhatsApp, Gmail and voice notes, transcribes locally with Whisper, extracts facts into a knowledge graph, and drafts speeches and briefings on demand. Built from four open-source pieces — NanoClaw, Mnemon, OneCLI, and Karpathy’s LLM wiki pattern — wired together with Claude via the Anthropic API.
He is a sitting cabinet minister. He did not hire a team. He composed it.

The lesson for executives isn’t the stack. The stack will be obsolete in months. The lesson is that the work was tool assembly, and that’s the skill that compounds. Standard RAG retrieves chunks of raw text; his system synthesises facts into a persistent graph. That distinction — between rented intelligence and owned memory — is where the productivity gap is opening for the next few years.

He even advises politicans to ‘get their hands dirty’ and try this tech, before making AI Policies. 

The new executive model isn’t “I use ChatGPT.” It’s “I built and operate the system that reasons over my work, on hardware I control.” Most leaders are still on the wrong side of that line.

posts.text:
I spent the last 6 weeks as AI Engineer Singapore’s professional stick chaser.

This is not my official title, but Rachael De Foe joked that it should be my LinkedIn byline, and honestly... true.

I was brought on to help primarily with logistics, which is just a cool way of saying I did all the unsexy stuff, like chasing speaker headshots, bios, talk titles, sponsor logos, booth assets, ordering swag, coordinating catering, and sorting through dozens of merch boxes that appeared at Sherry Jiang and 🥃 Agrim Singh's crib.

At some point, Sherry also joked that I had become her chief of staff because I knew, off the top of my head, all the things she needed to get done. Also actually true. 

The timelines were tight, the moving pieces kept multiplying, and everyone was doing this on top of full-time jobs. There were definitely moments where I looked at another Google sheet/Whatsapp group/Codex chat: why are we like this?

But honestly, it was also really, really fun.

Because AI Engineer Singapore was community-first in a way that felt very real.
Not community-first as a tagline, but community-first as in: we all actually like each other and want to spend time with one another, so we keep finding reasons to get together.

Impromptu late-night dim sum hosted by swyx. Zi char dinners. Drinks at my favourite bar. Speakers not wanting to leave. Some trying to figure out how to move to Singapore (cough Josh Newton we welcome you!). Even the Minister for Foreign Affairs cancelling his 9am so he could stay to listen to a few more talks after his.

That’s the part I keep coming back to.

This has always been about building connections. Building community. Creating spaces where people can meet each other, learn from each other, and realise they’re not building alone.

I got to see the very unglamorous side of making that happen, and if anything, it made me appreciate the whole thing even more.

Because care looks like the big moments on stage, yes. But it also looks like volunteers showing up early, speakers staying late to talk to students, sponsors backing something because they believe in the ecosystem, and a group of people obsessing over details because they want the room to feel generous, useful, and alive. 

I’m still processing the fact that we pulled this off.

Huge thank you to the sponsors, speakers, volunteers, partners, and every single person who believed in us and showed up. This only worked because so many people cared enough to make it real. I can't tag every single one of you but please know I appreciate you all so very much. 

See you in 2027!!! 

Ivan Leo Kaspar Hidayat Nehal Agrawal Brian C. 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan Daren T.

posts.text: Three days at AI Engineer Singapore changed how I think about building. I attended as one of the sponsored students selected by 65labs, and got to learn from people building the frontier of AI across software, design, research, and product. The biggest takeaway was not how fast AI is moving, but how much human judgment still matters in shaping what gets built. A few moments and conversations that stayed with me: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan - Minister for Foreign Affairs, Singapore: His talk on building a personal AI second brain was one of the strongest starts to the conference. The line that stuck with me most: “You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on.” You have to learn by doing. Thibault Sottiaux and Gabriel Chua - OpenAI / Codex: The Codex sessions showed how software engineering is shifting from writing code line by line to working with agents that can plan, execute, and check. We also got a glimpse into what the future of Codex could look like for the rest of 2026. Ryo Lu - Head of Design at Cursor: I had the chance to speak with Ryo after his talk and dig deeper into his design philosophy. His framing of “glass” over “black box” really stayed with me: tools should help us think together, stay in control, and build intuition. As AI generates more, design feels more important, not less. Phil Hedayatnia - Co-founder / CEO at Airfoil: Phil’s perspective on design in an AI-native world connected deeply with what I care about. During his workshop, I had the opportunity to speak with him 1-on-1 about the importance of original design as AI makes building faster and more accessible. Max Buckley - Head of Knowledge Research and Ishan Goswami - Founding Devrel Engineer, Exa: Meeting the Exa team and joining them for dinner was one of the best parts of the conference. Our conversations around search APIs, retrieval, and how agents interact with the internet opened my eyes to what AI systems need beyond just a good model. Geoffrey Huntley: I got the chance to meet Geoff backstage and have a 1.5-hour conversation about how AI is not just changing how we build software, but how companies themselves might operate. We also spoke about what the next generation needs to do to stay at the forefront of this shift. Sara Hooker- Co-founder at adaption: Sara’s talk on shaping the next era of intelligence reminded me that the future is not only about bigger models. We also got to meet her backstage and talk about adaptive systems, feedback, and how models that improve around real use cases may shape where AI goes next. Huge thank you to Rachael De Foe for making this opportunity possible and supporting the student cohort throughout the conference. Thank you as well to 65labs, Sherry Jiang, 🥃 Agrim Singh, and all the sponsors who made the student tickets possible. AI Engineer Singapore made one thing clear: The future of AI in Singapore is not something we just watch happen. It is something we build. And I’m excited to keep building. * +3 too good!!!! posts.text: I went in last night fully expecting the demos to fall apart halfway through. 💢 💻 Computer use agents are the kind of thing you sit through politely — half the demos drift into Safari opening itself, or the model getting stuck on a checkbox. That's where the tech still is on most days. So when Gabriel and I co-hosted OpenAI Codex Hack Night with Lorong AI last night — bring something, build it, demo it, no rails — I assumed we'd spend half the evening laughing at the failure modes. What actually happened was that the room used the time to chase curiosities, not benchmarks. Faye Li built a self-portrait of Codex in Blender. Not a script that imports a model — she had Codex driving Blender directly through computer use, modelling a little robot with a screen for a face and a keyboard for a body. The kind of thing you'd never spec out in a sprint planning meeting. Just an idea she wanted to see exist. Raymond used Codex to help him DJ directly with Djay Pro. No thoughts, just vibes, and Codex driving the musical tempo. Now even agents can help us unwind :) Another builder decided they wanted a dating agent that would filter for cute folks. Built it. Demo'd it. Room loved it. Neither of these is a "production AI use case." That's the point. What computer use actually seems to unlock — based on a packed Monday night at Lorong AI — isn't the polished agent that makes it to a keynote. It's the collapse of the gap between "huh, I wonder if I could…" and "let me just try." Curiosities that used to need a weekend now need an evening. Ideas that used to be too silly to start are now small enough to ship. That's the version of agentic Singapore I keep showing up for. Not the demos that look impressive on a slide — the ones built because someone in the room genuinely wanted to see what would happen. Huge thanks to Gabriel Chua and the Lorong AI team for the space and the energy, and to OpenAI for the credits that let people just play. If this sounds like your kind of room, aievents.sg has the rest of the Road to AIE lineup. And the main event — AI Engineer Singapore, May 15–17 at Capitol Kempinski, the first AI Engineer summit in Asia — kicks off this Friday. See you there. 🇸🇬 Brian C. Brendan Graetz 🪞Penélope Wan 萬砡君 Rach Pradhan Ace Yip Sherry Jiang 🥃 Agrim Singh Yuze Ma Ian S. Swedha Prabakaran Derek Wong Ryan Foo fire event, fire host!

4 years ago, #AI was just a curiosity I couldn’t stop thinking about. Not from the perspective of an engineer, but from a marketer who’s endlessly fascinated by how technology changes the way people create, communicate, and build. That curiosity somehow led me to volunteer at the AI Engineer Singapore event this week, and I’m still processing how inspiring the entire experience was. I met so many brilliant builders, founders, researchers, and genuinely kind humans who are shaping the future in ways both big and small. What surprised me most wasn’t just how smart everyone was, it was how open everyone was. Open to sharing ideas, encouraging experimentation, and welcoming people who are still figuring things out. That because I didn’t have an engineering degree, wasn’t technical enough, experienced enough, or building enough, I should stay on the sidelines. This experience challenged that belief completely. I’m walking away from this event feeling deeply grateful for the volunteer team, remarkable guests, the conversations, encouragement and this newfound support system I didn’t know I needed. posts.text:
AI Engineer SG 2026 felt like a glimpse into where AI is heading next.

Spent the first half of the day volunteering at the registration counter — battling the crowd and helping get everyone in — before finally getting to enjoy the talks, demos, and booths for the rest of the event.

A few ideas that really stuck with me:
1️⃣ Long-horizon tasks are becoming the real unlock for agents

The goal isn’t just “longer-running” agents.

It’s agents that can meaningfully improve outputs over time without constant human intervention — reliably, economically, and with good judgment.

Some practical ideas shared:
- Build checklists into the workflow
- Force verification after each step
- Give agents permission to pivot when needed

When done well, agents work while you rest.

2️⃣ A 1M token context window does NOT mean a model can reason well across 1M tokens

Managing context is very different from understanding context.

Compaction techniques help fit information into the window, but they don’t automatically preserve the most meaningful signals or relationships.

Felt like an important reminder that “more context” ≠ “better thinking”.

3️⃣ AI products need to optimise for one of two modes:
- synchronous deep work with humans
- asynchronous delegated work through agents

The awkward middle ground is where things start breaking down.
---
Really enjoyed meeting new people Matthew Tan Chloe C. Jie Hao (Tom) Tan Jin Yang 楊金 Jian Jie Liau 😸 Qi Jie Lim and reconnecting with old friends Kuang Wen Chan Freddie Lam ruban sk Suphasak U Alex Teo throughout the event.

posts.text:
What a weekend.

I was at ai.engineer Singapore, tagging along with Justin Baird FRSA for something that ended up being one of the most meaningful things I've been part of.

Funny how it started - literally a month ago, I woke up to a text from Siddharth asking me to meet a guy who needed BCI help. I reluctantly dragged myself out of bed. Met Justin. He painted a compelling vision (pun intended). I said yes.

Yesterday, that yes turned into Kai Ming - living with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome - controlling a robotic painting arm through her brain activity, live on stage at a packed conference. 

I've been asked before why I work on brain-computer interfaces. 

My answer has always been: I want to build a future where people have a closer relationship with technology - one where the machine meets you where you are, not the other way around.

Watching Kai Ming paint on stage, I felt that future arrive a little early. What she said about reconnecting with her passion for painting will stay with me for a long time.

That's what we're building at Mind Interface Company - the bridge between human intent and the world using AI.

posts.text: Honoured to be one of the 20 students selected to receive the student scholarship from 65labs to attend AI Engineer Singapore.🥰 It was an inspiring experience learning from engineers, builders, and teams working on the future of AI engineering, agentic systems, and developer tools. 3️⃣ key takeaways from today: 1. AI coding is moving beyond code generation - AI is no longer just helping developers autocomplete code. It is starting to support the full software development lifecycle, from planning and building to review, testing, and deployment. 2. Agent security should be designed around credential isolation and accountable execution - Instead of giving agents direct access to credentials, a stronger design is to keep zero credentials inside the agent environment itself. When approval is required, actions execute using the approver’s credentials instead, providing clearer identity, attribution, auditability, and accountability. 3. The future of coding agents is not just smarter models, but better systems around them - One thing I found especially interesting from the Codex sharing was how much engineering goes into the infrastructure around the model itself, sandboxing, orchestration, memory, auto-review, evaluation, and reliability. Huge thanks to Gavriel Cohen, founder of NanoClaw, for the insightful sharing on autonomous agents and secure AI systems. posts.text: Day 3 and the final day of AI Engineer Singapore! posts.text:
AI Engineer Singapore is exactly what you'd expect - demos, frameworks, agents doing increasingly impressive things. But the talks that landed hardest were the ones about where AI stops, and where humans come in.

Dr Vivian Balakrishnan (Singapore's Foreign Minister) put it simply: you can outsource memory and computation, but you cannot outsource understanding. In his words, "You cannot govern a technology you've only been briefed on."

Sara Hooker (Co-founder, adaption) argued that scaling monolithic LLMs is hitting a wall. The next phase is smaller, efficient models that adapt to context in real-world situations, using compute proportional to the task. As models get more capable, the question shifts from how powerful they are to how well humans deploy them.

Tejas Kumar (Developer Advocate, IBM) made that concrete: with the right harness around a model - prompts, tools, structure - you can get strong results even from weaker models. The bottleneck isn't the model. It's the system built around it.

Gavriel Cohen (Creator, NanoClaw) took that to its logical end: agents do the work, but whoever presses approve is accountable. The agent runs with your credentials. Capability doesn't dissolve responsibility; it concentrates it.

Huge thanks to the 65labs team for organising an excellent conference, and to all sponsors who made the student tickets possible. I really enjoyed meeting and learning from everyone - speakers and students alike.

The ceiling on AI isn't a technical problem. It's a human one - understanding, judgment, accountability. These values aren't getting automated away. They're becoming the constraint.

posts.text: Wrapping up AI Week in Singapore, what a week it has been! 💻 The week started at the Claude Code: Beyond the Basics, held by Women Devs SG. The focus wasn’t on prompt tricks, but on engineering discipline for agentic workflows. We went deep into Spec Driven Development (SDD), how the importance of Test Driven Development (TDD) increased in this Agentic AI era, how hooks and guardrails make agents safe, predictable, and ultimately product higher quality code An interesting question brought up is how we can further optimize context management by using CLIs through progressive disclosure instead of MCPs, although I’ve also been reading about how harnesses from Claude/Codex has been improving on this front on handling MCP’s context efficiency, so perhaps MCPs aren’t dead after all 🤔 On Saturday, I joined a fireside chat hosted by Cursor During the session, I had the opportunity to share with the audience about my shift towards SDD and Harness Engineering at work. Engineers should design the architecture and constraints, generating concrete specs and architectural / code quality constraints for agents to reference before they handle implementation. It was also great learning how other developers are using other open source tools to enhance their agentic workflow such as Greptile for reviews and Granola for taking notes that can be converted straight into PRDs 🤯 Finally, I wrapped up the week at AI Engineer Singapore, as a volunteering crew member, but also had the chance to listen to talks that share so many novel ideas from inspirational speakers in Google DeepMind, OpenAI and many YC Combinator AI startup founders. One of the biggest takeaways among many others, is the shift from “improving prompts” towards Harness Engineering. About how we don’t have to improve our prompt, but instead improve the environment and context built BY our agents, FOR our agents to work better with our SAME prompt. The AI space is evolving faster every day. And to stay ahead, it’s ever so important to know how to adapt to this ever changing environment, how to better use AI. 💯 Most importantly, I’m so so grateful for the conversations, people, and ideas shared this week!! 🚀

posts.text: Day 1 at AI Engineer Singapore 🧠 Notes from workshops by Stripe, AWS, Vercel, Convex, Arize 1. AEO is the new SEO — your product needs to show up in AI responses, not just Google. 2. Evals are your moat — without them, switching models = weeks of manual testing. With them = hours. 3. The eval loop that separates production teams from everyone else: Instrument → Trace → Evaluate → Annotate → Analyze → Fix & Deploy → repeat. 4. Agents need money — Stripe is building KYA (Know Your Agent), wallets, and HTTP 402 as a payment primitive. AWS AgentCore is shipping the production runtime, memory, observability. The agent economy has rails now. 5. Schema-first is non-negotiable. Agents infer the modelling predictably based on schema. Get it wrong early, pay for it forever. 6. DB layer is evolving too — AI agents work well with transactional backends that handle real-time mutations and queries without blocking on 3rd party AI models communicated though websockets. 7. Performance plateaus — after enough prompt/RAG/model experiments, you stop improving on the same axis. The unlock is injecting new ideas to the agents with (e.g. research papers), not more iterations. The fundamental pieces are in place. The infrastructure is here. The industry just needs to catch up — and keep iterating. # AI Engineer Singapore Notes from Stripe AWS Vercel Workshops This title was summarized by AI from the post below.

Caught a slice of AI Engineer Singapore this week, and my scratchpad is full.

A few takeaways from where I sit as an SRE looking at AI through the lens of running enterprise agents in production:

Agent observability is no longer optional. If you’re shipping agents and can’t see what they’re doing, you’re flying blind. Simple as that.

Evaluations are where most of us are earlier than we like to admit. Tracing is everywhere; disciplined evals are not. That gap is where production quality quietly leaks. I left with a much sharper view of what “good” looks like here.

The coding harness itself is becoming an observable surface. Watching teams instrument Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex as first-class agents to trace and evaluate genuinely shifted how I think about AI-augmented engineering at scale.

But the real highlight? The candour in the room. Enterprise practitioners, SMEs, and startup founders trading real war stories — owning the messy bits, sharing what worked and what didn’t. That kind of honesty is rare, and I left every conversation a little sharper than I walked in.

Big thanks to the Arize AI team for the invite, and to the organisers for pulling together an event that actually moved the conversation forward. Already looking forward to next year! 🚀

Patrick Kelly, Sean Lee, Jin Yang 楊金 , SallyAnn DeLucia, Sangyoul Jin

posts.text: Builders. Practitioners. Policymakers. All in one room. One thing that genuinely stood out at AI Engineer Singapore today was seeing Vivian Balakrishnan not just talk about AI… but actually build with it. He spoke about running NanoClaw personally, containerisation, privacy, memory systems, semantic search, Raspberry Pi deployments, WhatsApp-based agents, Obsidian knowledge graphs, and the importance of understanding technology hands-on instead of governing it from PowerPoint slides. A few takeaways that stayed with me: • “You cannot govern a technology that you have only been briefed on.” Probably one of the strongest messages of the day. • AI becomes truly useful when connected to personal context and memory. Not just chat. Not just prompts. Persistent memory, relationships, semantic understanding. • Accessibility matters. Hearing that one of his daily-use agents runs on an old Raspberry Pi with 8GB RAM was refreshing in a world obsessed with massive infrastructure. • The future is likely hybrid. LLMs + deterministic systems + symbolic reasoning working together instead of “LLMs for everything.” • Privacy and containerisation are becoming critical design principles. Especially as agents become more autonomous and deeply integrated into our lives. What impressed me most was the mindset, which I believe as well and have been practicing: - learn by doing. - experiment personally. - understand the limits as much as the potential. This wasn’t a generic “AI will change the world” keynote. It felt like hearing from someone actively trying to operationalize AI into real daily workflows under real-world constraints. We are living through a very interesting shift where AI is no longer only for engineers. Builders are emerging everywhere. Curious mind. Builder mode! 🇸🇬 #AIEngineer #Singapore #AI #Agents #OpenSource #LLM #AIEngineering #NanoClaw #DeveloperTools #Innovation 👍
