Inspired by Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs in a recent talk on “Building a ‘Second Brain’: Opportunities, Risks, and Implications for AI Adoption in Singapore,” I was reminded of the importance of practical experience, deliberate practice, and continuous application over theory alone.

On a lighter note, there was also a point about how almost everything can be outsourced, but not your understanding and accountability. It echoes a thought I’ve often had: in a globalised world where import, export, and outsourcing are normal, what remains truly non-transferable is your own heart, mind, and discipline.

The key takeaway for me is simple but powerful: learning is not passive. It is built through doing, refining, failing, and repeating with intent.
I’ve summarised the speech using NotebookLM for my own learning and motivation, and I’m sharing this to encourage others to stay consistent with their goals, whether things are going smoothly or not.

If anything is missing or misinterpreted in my summary, I sincerely apologise. The full context and depth can be better appreciated through the original YouTube video linked below.

- Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan: You cannot govern a technology you've only been briefed on. Get hands-on.

- Ryo Lu  (Cursor): Thanks for the sharing for design tips. 

- Gavriel Cohen  (Nanoclaw): Zero credentials in agent env.
· Governance (GovTech): 1.3B agents by 2028. Sovereign agentic harness.

- Phil Hedayatnia  (Airfoil): Design for the deciding, not just the decision.

- Annie L.  (Google): Build exploration, not just execution.

- Jimmy Lai  (Vercel): Every prototype that survives becomes something a person has to maintain.

Had a great time with team Exa alongside with Bernardino Lintang K Jagateesvaran Rajoo Aditya Arya Max Buckley Ishan Goswami Sam Mitchell  . 

- JJ Geewax  (DeepMind): "Models aren't magic." Small focused chunks + determinism. Had a great time talking about world model and with a lovely student Lavanya Garg 
 
- Sara Hooker : Scaling era is over. Next era = adaptability. Thanks for taking time to talk with us! 

- Geoffrey Huntley : Build your own agents. Don't just consume.

- Bhavan Jaipragas (Straits Times) Thanks for taking time to talk with the students and sharing your knowledge. 

- Yuzhang FENG (Ph.D.)  (GovTech) Government must evolve from AI-enabled to AI-native, 1.3 billion agents by 2028. Sovereign agentic harness: MCP gateway, sandboxed runtime, agent identity, memory, observability, skills platform.

- Gabriel Chua (OpenAI): Thanks for the demo that helps me understand the capability of codex and how we can use codex in our day to day life to improve efficiency.

The bottom line: Intelligence is becoming modular, adaptive, and human-centered. Winners won't have the biggest models — they'll make adaptation efficient.

posts.text:
It's easy to feel like AI is a rat race right now. New tools every day, everyone shipping, everyone posting, everyone one step ahead. I've felt that weight. But I volunteered at AI Engineer last weekend and here are the human stories, hiding in the margins of all the hustle.

It was nostalgic to be back at Singapore Management University . The week started with workshops and I sat in on a few, but what inspired me was meeting a group of 5 volunteers from KL.  Hong Bing Sim Bede Lau They'd won multiple hackathons already and built their own stuff (they're only 19-24) and still chose to fly in and volunteer, just to learn and be in the room. No agenda and just pure hunger. That energy set the tone for the rest of my week! 

Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan shared how he built his second brain workflows. A sitting minister, talking about personal AI systems. Singapore's leadership isn't just making policy about AI they're using it and that says something about where this country is headed. 

Saturday at Capitol Kempinski was the main conference. 2000+ people. Robotics demos, agent infrastructure, product showcases. A chance encounter with Xingyi Li whose phone was dying — turns out she was helping to manage one of the robotics booths. She'd actually featured crochet characters her grandmother knitted at the booth. A nod to her grandma, right there next to cutting-edge robotics, just like how I've been trying to build something for my grandmother with AI. We landed on the same thing — AI should be empowering people who don't have access to it yet. That's been my thread all week.

At Project6 's meetup, I met Skyler Hong building in Physical AI. Wearable gloves that collect data from cleaners, factory workers, anyone on the ground. AI meeting people where they actually work. Zo Computer has been killing it all week at their demos, showing how content creators, hair salons and small businesses leverage AI to build a $100k stream income. 

At a coffee meetup prepping for a hackathon with Gao Min Mell and Kari Tamura Chua we struck up a conversation with Jeremy Lee (he sat beside us by chance!) a founder who spends his Fridays personally automating workflows for his employees, trying to get them to see what AI can do. The founder, doing the convincing and manual work of improving workflows for his employees! That's really inspiring. 

Varick Lim , a content creator I'd known mutually but finally connected with properly. We're creatives at heart, and there's a lot of technical stuff within the AI space, but sometimes we're so focused on ROI-positive outcomes in AI that we strip out the soul, the fun. The crossover between creative work and engineering is where something special lives, and we keep optimising it away.

This week reminded me that behind all the noise, there are real people building for real reasons and that's the energy worth protecting! Not the rat race, but the human one. 

📸 Swipe for the week.

posts.text:
Singapore’s Foreign Minister, Vivian Balakrishnan runs his second brain on a Raspberry Pi with 8GB of RAM.

He showed the whole stack at the AI Engineer Summit last week, walking through it for twenty minutes without a single slide on theory. NanoClaw with Baileys handling his WhatsApp  comms, Mnemon for graph memory, Ollama  running embeddings locally, Whisper for voice capture, Obsidian sitting on top as the wiki layer. He built it himself, on hardware that costs less than a business class lunch in Changi, and he uses it every day to think.

The line that has stayed with me since: “You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on.”

That sentence describes the gap I see in almost every executive conversation across APJ right now, where leaders are commissioning AI strategies they have never personally used the underlying tools to build, signing off on operating models they could not describe at the level of a single workflow if asked to. The briefing deck has quietly replaced the hands-on hour, and most boards seem comfortable with that trade.

Balakrishnan’s argument is not that every executive should learn to deploy containers. His point is that direct contact with the technology has become part of the governance job, because without it the risk frameworks turn into performance and the operating model design stays one full layer abstracted from the thing it is meant to govern.

If a sitting Foreign Minister can find the time to run Ollama and Mnemon on a Pi in his own kitchen, the question for the rest of us is no longer about capacity. It is about willingness to do the work ourselves, on cheap hardware, in the evenings, until we actually understand what we are accountable for.

Uploaded the entire speech on my X.

OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Cursor, Vercel, Stripe, Cognition, Z.ai, and many more were in the room.

The front seats were not for them.
I still don’t know how to explain what that felt like.

There were ministers, founders, researchers, engineers behind the tools we use every day, and people I had only seen online. Anyone in that room could have been made to feel like the most important person there.

65labs chose the students.

Not symbolically.

We had reserved seats.
We had scheduled meetups with speakers after their talks.
We got to ask questions directly.

Even when someone could not be there in person, like Thibault Sottiaux (Tibo) from OpenAI, Rachael made sure our questions reached him and were answered.

When she realised some of us were travelling all the way from NTU, even our cabs were covered. It may sound small, It was not.

At every step, the message was the same:

You should be here. 
Not someday. 
Now.

A student ticket can be sponsored. What 65labs did went far beyond that. They showed us what believing in students actually looks like.

In Agrim’s closing talk, he said something that has stayed with me:

You are the scene.
Keep showing up. Keep building. Don’t wait for permission to share your work.

I have kept a lot of my own work offline for a long time. Things I built, events I attended, hackathons, people I met, lessons I should have shared.

AI Engineer Singapore made me realise it was time to stop keeping everything quiet.

So this is where I start.

Thank you, 65labs.

Thank you, Rachael, Sherry, Agrim and every builder who helped open the door for the 20 of us:  Ainul Md Razib, Patrick Kelly, Neil Chang, Hsu Ken Ooi, Ivan Leo, Kaspar Hidayat, Zayne Zhang, and others.

I will write about AI Engineer Singapore separately.

This first one is for the people who made sure students were not watching from outside the room.

posts.text: AI Engineer Singapore. The energy in the room. The cracked engineers. The people moving the needle. The people building. I can’t fully put it into words, but once you see it, you know the ceiling is much higher than what you thought. Here are some of my takeaways: 1. You can’t govern a technology you have only been briefed on That was probably one of the most prominent takeaways from Dr Vivian Balakrishnan’s speech. Because it is fundamentally true. You can’t strategize effectively around something you don’t understand. You can’t decide where to take your product next if you don’t know what the technology is good at, where it breaks, and what it makes possible. And this is not just about using ChatGPT and attaching a few MCP connectors. It is about building. Because when you build, you understand how agents actually work underneath the hood. 2. Ground-up value creation Another point that stood out was the idea of ground-up value creation. Real AI impact does not happen only through top-down strategy. It happens when people start applying AI to real problems in their own work. Individual by individual. Workflow by workflow. Team by team. Broad AI strategy matters, but the real test is whether the use of AI creates better experiences, improves outcomes, and delivers real value to end users. 3. This is the era of builders If you have an idea, ship it. If you see a user problem, build for it. There’s a phrase: “Ideas are cheap, execution is everything.” Guess what? Execution on building products has become cheaper too. The cost of going from idea to prototype has collapsed. The tools are better. The feedback loops are shorter. The barrier to building is lower. You no longer need a huge team or months of planning just to test whether something can work. Tiny teams can now build, ship, and iterate at a speed that used to be impossible. That means the advantage now goes to people who are willing to build, test, learn, and iterate quickly. And as the quote goes: “The best way to predict the future is to create it.” So what’s stopping us? 4. Spectrum of AI literacy There is a spectrum of AI literacy across and outside the industry. Some people are not using the tools because of skepticism. Some people only know AI as ChatGPT. And some people are driving the progress of these tools on a day-to-day basis. Even within the AI industry, there is a huge disparity. There are people wiring up a few tools and calling it an agent. There are people who fundamentally understand how agents, harnesses, tools, and skills work. And then there is a whole other level: the people in frontier labs pushing the industry forward. One reason this knowledge gap exists is that AI is moving incredibly fast, and it is becoming harder to keep up. My notes are full of thoughts and ideas. Here’s to building and getting things done. Let’s get it.

posts.text: Three insights I took away from AI Engineer Singapore: 1. For my own work, I may become 60% AI coordinator and 40% AI engineer. After watching the OpenAI Codex demos — from controlling a computer via a phone to building and running a real-time translation app in under 5 minutes — I felt that more of my time might shift toward deciding what to build, while AI handles more of the implementation. 2. AI / LLM evaluation may become a core part of my role. The Arize AI session made me realize that, for my own work, building AI applications may not be enough. A big part of my role may be evaluating whether LLM systems are actually working well: tracing, debugging, measuring quality, and improving them through production feedback loops. 3. Programming language may no longer be the biggest barrier. During the Mastra TypeScript AI Agent Framework session, only about 10% of attendees had TypeScript experience. But with AI-assisted development, what mattered more was understanding the workflow and system design. Of course, engineering fundamentals still matter. But this event made me reflect on my own direction: I may need to grow as an AI coordinator as much as an AI engineer — someone who can define the problem, guide the tools, evaluate the results, and connect everything into a working system. #AIEngineering #LLMEvaluation #AgenticAI #AIEngineerSingapore

posts.text:
Two days into AI Engineer Singapore, the strongest signal is not “use more agents.”

It is this: Most teams are not ready for agents yet.

Not because the models are weak. Because the factory around the model is weak.

I kept hearing the same idea from different angles.

Daytona session was about infrastructure for agents: sandboxes, security, model choice, context recycling, and the danger of letting vendors own the layer your agents run on.

Exa workshop showed search becoming structured context for agents. Not search results for humans. Search results as markdown, rendered outputs, PDFs, and reliable inputs that agents can consume.

Cursor “agent factory” framing hit the hardest for me: the factory is harder to build than the product.

You need specs. Skills. READMEs. Test environments. Clear phases. Parallel tasks. Sequential tasks. PR review loops. Agents that can complain when the workflow is bad.

If the agent goes off the rails, that is not only an agent problem. It is a factory problem.

The OpenAI Codex pointed in the same direction: explicitly spawn subagents, use skills, turn memory on, use docs, create hooks, and give the agent a better operating environment.

One thing felt almost universally accepted: the human is no longer needed to type most of the code.

That does not remove the human from the process. It moves the human upstream.

The work shifts from writing every line to designing the system where agents can write, test, fail, recover, and ship safely.

My takeaway: the next advantage is not having an agent. Everyone will have agents.

The advantage is having a system where agents can actually work.

Context. Sandboxes. Tests. Permissions. Memory. Specs. Observability. Human checkpoints.

This is why I’m becoming more interested in software factories than coding agents.

A coding agent is useful. A software factory can change how a whole team builds.

Are you building one? Drop a comment.

AI Engineer Singapore가 오늘 마무리되었습니다. 직접 듣지는 못했지만 개인적으로 이번 행사에서 가장 인상깊었던 장면은 바로 싱가포르 외교부장관 비비안 발라크리쉬난 박사의 발표였던 것 같습니다. 

정부에 몸담고 있으면서 직접 NanoClaw를 써서 Raspberry Pi에 개인비서 에이전트를 구축한 이야기는 여러모로 시사하는 바가 많은 것 같습니다. 젠슨 황, 데미스 하사비스, 다리오 아모데이 등 대부분의 리더들이 오래전부터 AI 규제의 필요성을 이야기했지만 실제로 규제를 만드는 입법부와 규제를 실행하는 정부쪽의 움직임은 잘 포착이 되지 않아왔습니다. 

비비안 장관은 이렇게 말했다고 합니다. "우리가 잘 모르는 것을 제대로 규제할 수 있겠느냐" 제 개인적으로는 정말 사막에서 오아시스를 만난 것 같이 반가운 말이었습니다. 전문가를 불러서 이야기를 듣는 데서 멈추지 않고 직접 손을 움직여서 뭔가를 만들어본 리더라면, 어디까지가 실제 현재 기술로 가능하고 어디까지가 마케팅을 위해 과장되었는지 구분할 수 있을 것이기 때문입니다.

지난 2024년 12월 젠슨 황 Nvidia CEO가 한 인터뷰에서 "정부는 단순히 규제만을 강제하는 게 아니라 직접 AI를 사용하는 사용자가 되어야 한다"고 말한 바 있는데, 2026년 5월 싱가포르에서 이렇게 현실이 되었네요. 이번 비비안 박사의 발표를 계기로 앞으로 더 많은 시도와 배움이 공공분야에서 보이면 참 좋겠다는 바람을 가져봅니다.

Day 2 done.

Same system as Day 1. 35 more talks, 500+ slides, 80,000+ words of transcripts. Same digest pattern — decoded, summarised, indexed by why each talk matters.

https://lnkd.in/gwM7FbHu

Three patterns surfaced when I read Day 1 and Day 2 back-to-back:

✅ The orchestration consensus from Day 1 became the canon by Day 2. 

Tejas Kumar (IBM) named the six harness primitives. JJ Geewax (Google DeepMind) gave the load-bearing frame — surround the non-deterministic model with deterministic boundaries. Henry Mao (Smithery) coined the harness era of agent agency. When the argument stops being made and the work becomes operational, the bet has shipped.

✅ The next moat is one layer down — data and eval. 

Sara Hooker (Adaption Labs) called it directly: scaling is over, the rate of return moved. SallyAnn DeLucia (Arize) on planning-state infra. Timothy Lin (Resaro) selling sovereign-grade evals into Temasek, DSTA, GovTech. The robotics block converged on the same line.

✅ Singapore wasn't the venue. Singapore was the operator bench. 

Tusk, Resaro, Lightsprint, Smithery, Hyperspell — SG founders dominated the harness layer of Day 2.

posts.text:
You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on.
That was the key message.

At AI Engineer Singapore, Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan shared how he uses NanoClaw to communicate with his AI assistant through WhatsApp.

The point was not novelty.

It was cognitive overload.

He said that in one month, he was visiting 12 countries, meeting hundreds of people, and needing to understand each country’s economy, geography, culture, history, conflicts and personalities.

That is where AI becomes interesting.

Not as a chatbot.

But as a working memory system.

A second brain that helps organise information, retrieve context, and support real work.

AI literacy is no longer just knowing how to prompt.

It is understanding how agents, memory, workflows and governance come together.

You need to understand what it feels like when the tool becomes part of the work.

You need to experience how it changes the work itself.

"𝑌𝑜𝑢 𝑐𝑎𝑛𝑛𝑜𝑡 𝑔𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑛 𝑎 𝑡𝑒𝑐ℎ𝑛𝑜𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑦 𝑡ℎ𝑎𝑡 𝑦𝑜𝑢 ℎ𝑎𝑣𝑒 𝑜𝑛𝑙𝑦 𝑏𝑒𝑒𝑛 𝑏𝑟𝑖𝑒𝑓𝑒𝑑 𝑜𝑛."

That was the closing line that Claude wrote for Minister for Foreign Affairs Dr Vivian Balakrishnan during his opening speech at AI Engineer Singapore. He spoke about how he built his own open-source "second brain" using NanoClaw to manage information. 

True mastery requires getting your hands dirty. This resonated deeply because I have been spending the last couple of weeks doing that: building my first Telegram bot for family management.

Here are the three major takeaways:

𝟏) 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐛𝐞 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐝
You can delegate tasks and computation to AI, but you cannot outsource your own conceptual understanding. AI didn't replace my learning, but accelerated it. I still had to understand what I was building and troubleshoot when things broke.

𝟐) 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥
Macro policies are essential, but the true payoff happens workflow by workflow. It is driven by ordinary professionals re-engineering their daily routines. AI gives non-technical people the tools and confidence to build something real right now.

𝟑) 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐮𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐬𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐛𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐠
The essential tools have already been invented. This is the future of lifelong learning, where we don't just attend formal courses, but active, AI-assisted experimentation.

The barriers to entry have collapsed. The future belongs to the builders and practitioners who are willing to look stupid, ask questions, and create. What are you building today?

The science says otherwise. Cognitive capacity fluctuates with sleep debt, hormonal cycles, and training load. Yet no planner accounts for any of it.
Cadence does.

posts.text:
Ministers in Governments all over the world, will now be able to let the public see ALL of their decisions and activities, thanks to this new Sovereign AI technology 🔥

Singapore’s Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan just did something no sitting minister has ever done…

He published the source code of the AI assistant he built and uses every day. 

It runs on a Raspberry Pi, hooks into his WhatsApp and Gmail, transcribes his voice notes, drafts his speeches, and gets smarter over time.  

He calls it his “second brain for a diplomat.” 

His words: “You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on.” 

and he means it literally.

What makes this remarkable isn’t the technology. It’s the architecture philosophy. Voice notes are transcribed on-device, vector embeddings run locally, and each messaging group gets its own isolated container, meaning no sensitive content ever leaves his network.  

For MPs and ministers, this matters enormously. 

Cloud-based AI tools mean your briefings, policy positions, and constituent conversations sit on someone else’s server. 

A self-hosted, local-first setup gives you the full power of AI with none of the data sovereignty risk…it’s the only model that’s actually fit for public office.

In his own words, “the barriers to entry have come down so dramatically, everyone should embark on their personal experiments” 

he proved it by running this on a Raspberry Pi with 8GB of RAM that’s at least two years old.  

This isn’t a government moonshot or a million-dollar procurement. 

It’s an accessible, open-source blueprint any MP could replicate this weekend. 

The question isn’t whether AI will reshape governance…in fact, it already is. 

The question is : are your representatives are building it, or just being briefed on it?

Watch this video for more info 👾

[Singaporean Pride, and a Commentary on AI] One of the reasons why I am a proud Singaporean, and want to do my level best to plant the Singapore 🇸🇬 flag globally in my humble way. Singapore is known for good governance. But what makes good governance tick is not flowery language, but understanding what we govern. And understanding what we govern means we must dabble with what we govern. And given how almost every PMET job in Singapore has been disrupted with AI, it means almost every PMET has to understand AI, and to understand AI we have to tinker and gain personal insights through our tinkering. That is what Foreign Minister Dr. Vivian Balakrisnan mentioned at the 65labs AI Engineer conference (I caught the keynote on Youtube, and was unfortunately not at the conference itself). If the Minister can tinker with NanoClaw, understand how containerisation brings security benefit as opposed to OpenClaw, and publicises the project on his own Github, I realised I can do better. 😉 Highly, highly inspirational. Listening to the keynote in full (https://lnkd.in/gHKRQ9Ps) is highly recommended. #AI #walkingthetalk #leadership (Disclaimer: Not AI-drafted. I wanted to write this myself because it is an opportunity to go slow, and think of what I want to write. We should use AI to augment our thinking, and provide refinement, but not replace our personal experiences and accountability; these are the two aspects that AI cannot, and should never replace.)

“You cannot govern a technology you’ve only been briefed on.” This morning, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan walked into a room full of builders and did something that genuinely mattered: …he showed up as one himself He opened up his actual workflow, talked through the second brain he’s been building, the tradeoffs, the implications, the limits, and the things he’s still figuring out. And I’m sure, before he spoke, there were skeptics in the room. Builders have heard enough people talk about technology from a distance to know the difference between someone who has touched the tools and someone who has only read summaries about them. What struck me most wasn’t even the talk itself, it was what happened after He stayed. He went off stage and spent time with young builders. Students. Engineers. People still figuring out their place in all of this. Then he stayed in the room to watch Gavriel Cohen’s creator of NanoClaw talk because he genuinely wanted to hear it. And as someone on the organising team, I can tell you that none of it was staged and all of it was him. That detail will stay with me for a long time. There were students sitting in the front row today who now have a completely different reference point for what leadership can look like. He wasn’t speaking above the work. He was actually doing it. I’m very aware that what happened today was much bigger than us. Thank you, Minister Vivian Balakrishnan. Putting together 65labs AI Engineer has always been rooted in a hope that Singapore can become a place where serious builders collide openly, generously, and ambitiously. Today, you helped us show that it already is.

* +1

posts.text:
My biggest takeaway from the AI Engineer Singapore conference this year:

AI is no longer just about better models. It is becoming a systems design problem.

A few ideas stayed with me:

1. Agents are coming, but agents alone are not the strategy.  
One slide referenced IDC’s estimate of 1.3 billion AI agents by 2028. The real question is not “Can we add agents?” It is “Where do agents create leverage, and where do they add complexity?”

2. Ideas are becoming execution.  
When software becomes faster and cheaper to build, implementation is no longer the main bottleneck. Judgment is. What is worth building? What should be measured? What should be discarded?

3. Removing waste from systems may be a bigger accelerator than AI itself.  
If the workflow is broken, AI may simply accelerate the mess. Clean process design still matters.

4. Stop using the LLM as one giant problem-solver.  
Use LLMs for language, reasoning, classification, and generation. Use deterministic systems for routing, rules, consistency, and compliance.

A production-ready pattern is not one giant prompt. It is input → router → predefined route → structured transformation → generation → safety check → output.

5. Evaluation has to come first.  
Evals are becoming the modern version of test-driven development. Before fine-tuning, prompt optimization, or adding more agents, teams need golden datasets and clear success metrics.

6. Models are incredible, but they are not magic.  
Safety, compliance, observability, redaction, monitoring, release testing, and domain review still need to exist around the model.

7. For subjective decisions, good AI should design for the deciding, not just the decision.  
The first wave of AI removed friction. But for taste, style, identity, travel, shopping, and creative work, some friction is useful. Users need exploration, comparison, and confidence — not just one auto-generated answer.

My final takeaway:

The winning AI products will not simply be the ones with the biggest models or the most agents. They will be the ones that remove real waste, use LLMs where they are strongest, evaluate rigorously, and turn fast execution into disciplined learning.

Spent the weekend at the “Road to AI Engineers” event in Singapore — and as someone who is definitely not a coder (maybe a nerd, but certainly a CFO), it was genuinely eye-opening.

What struck me most was not the technology itself, but how quickly AI is moving from “interesting tool” to becoming core infrastructure for governments, businesses, and everyday work.

A few standout moments and takeaways:
🔹 Dr Vivian Balakrishnan’s opening address was particularly impactful.
 Hearing how he personally uses AI agents to improve productivity and effectiveness as Singapore’s Foreign Minister made the conversation around AI feel very real and practical — not theoretical. https://lnkd.in/gDKCtrTM
  
🔹 GovTech’s vision was crystal clear:
Singapore aims to become AI-native, not just AI-enabled
Government officers are actively being trained to use AI and agentic workflows
That distinction between enabled and native stayed with me.

🔹 Some interesting sessions and tools:
Nanocloud → reinforced how critical sandboxing and governance are in an AI-first world
Zo Computer → an interesting analogy around “peasants and kings” in SaaS evolution
Cursor → impressive platform for AI-assisted deployment and development
Vercel → very strong on UI and frontend deployment capabilities
(And yes… my Plaud AI companion captured notes from most of the sessions 😄)

My biggest reflections from the event:
1️⃣ AI is absolutely here to stay
 Singapore is investing heavily to bring the entire ecosystem forward — starting with government agencies.
2️⃣ Use AI purposefully
 AI is powerful, but also resource intensive. The focus should be on solving meaningful problems, not building frivolous applications for the sake of hype.
3️⃣ The possibilities are limitless — and so is the disruption
 The long-term impact remains uncertain, but one thing is clear: individuals and organisations that adapt early will have a significant advantage.

At aNew Energy, we are already exploring practical AI applications through our work with AutogenAI (https://autogenai.com/) , helping organisations prepare and submit tenders more effectively and efficiently — while improving win rates. Ping me if you are keen on AutogenAI.

Purposeful AI must be our motto!

Kudos to the https://www.65labs.org/ team! You rock and lets roll onward with AI!

I am a creative. Not a developer. I don't write code for a living. So when I walked into Ralphthon, an AI hackathon run by token maxxing and funded by OpenAI during AI Engineer Singapore... I had no idea what I was doing there. 

The rule was simple: if you touch your laptop, you wear a lobster costume. Your AI agent codes. You just... direct it.

In one day, I built Cari, an autonomous agent that helps Singapore caregivers find every government grant and subsidy they qualify for, from a single plain-English message/voice chat. No jargon. No social worker required.

This video is about what it actually feels like to be a creative person in a room full of engineers. The impostor syndrome. The moments it clicks. The realisation that knowing how to think, write, and communicate a problem clearly is not a soft skill, it's the skill that makes AI agents work.

If you're an artist, designer, writer, or creative who has been watching the AI space from the outside thinking it's not for you, well, it may not ever be... but for me, I learned. :)

posts.text:
AI Threat Intelligence Briefing (May 3–17, 2026)
 - 548 raw items collected → 42 final entries in the newsletter
 - 8 news, 8 vulnerabilities, 10 advisories, 8 papers, 8 tools

[Content Brief]
- Learning Moment — Singapore's Foreign Minister Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan built and runs NanoClaw — a self-hosted Claude assistant — on a single Raspberry Pi 5, shared at AI Engineer Singapore (16 May). It's a clean reference for securing an LLM agent: proxied credentials, per-group Docker isolation, mount/sender allowlists, on-device embeddings and transcription. His line — "you cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on" — is also a good pratice tip.

- Governance & Regulation: The Five Eyes agencies issued agentic-AI adoption guidance (now the AEGIS framework), and Singapore's CSA released rare out-of-cycle guidance on "frontier model risks." Regulators are still catching up — critics call the EU AI Act unprepared for autonomous agents, US Treasury pushed AI-governance alignment on financial institutions, and Colorado replaced its 2024 AI law.

- Vulnerabilities in the Wild: Critical flaws dominated — a CVSS 10.0 hardcoded JWT secret in SOCFortress CoPilot (CVE-2026-42869), unauthenticated RCE in FastGPT's agent-sandbox (CVE-2026-42302), and a cluster of insecure-deserialization torch.load() bugs across ML frameworks (ART, Ludwig, Mamba — all
 9.8). The "Mini Shai-Hulud" worm hit npm/PyPI packages from TanStack, Mistral AI and Guardrails AI — reaching OpenAI employee devices — while AWS and Microsoft patched SageMaker integrity and Copilot spoofing bugs.

- Research & Tools: New research formalized response-path attacks on BYOK agents and "termination poisoning" (LoopTrap) on autonomous loops, with ARGUS and MIPIAD proposing prompt-injection defenses. Notable OSS: Adrian (agent runtime monitoring), promptbeat (red-teaming), AiSOC (AI-powered SOC), and Cisco's foundry-security-spec.

#AISecurity #AppSec #AIGovernance #AgenticAI #LiteLLM #CyberSecurity

posts.text:
#AIEngineer was in town this weekend! 3 things that stood out.

1️⃣ Getting things done 1️⃣ 
65Labs is a collective that built a network of over 5,000 people in Singapore through meetups, workshops, and hackathons. 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang, and the team turned that energy into Singapore's first AI Engineer conference in three months. 

It was not only awesomely received, but the biggest brands in the space, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Cursor, etc., also backed it. They consistently built trust over two years; they didn't wait around for permission. They just got things done. #Inspired

2️⃣ Making knowledge accessible 2️⃣ 
The main panel was streamed. That's a small decision with real consequences: it means the conversation doesn't stay inside the room.

In a space that talks a lot about democratising access, they actually walked the talk and did it. This one meant a ton to me 🙏 And it was truly refreshing. 

3️⃣ Public Service can leverage it too 3️⃣ 
When Minister Vivian Balakrishnan shared his personal AI setup. Not a policy speech, not a vision statement. An actual system: raw sources ingested from transcripts, web clips, and voice notes; a knowledge graph extracting synthesised facts locally; wiki pages as the output layer, surfaced in Obsidian. All running on a Raspberry Pi 5, assembled from open source tools.

And the security architecture was the part I kept thinking about. Zero credentials stored in the agent environment. An approval gate where the human approves before any action executes with credentials. The design principle: it can't leak what it doesn't have.

That's not someone saying "AI is exciting." That's someone who has thought carefully about what responsible adoption looks like when the stakes are real, and then built something that reflects that thinking.

The railguards weren't an afterthought. They were the design. For those of us in public service, that's the model worth studying.

It was a fun weekend! ✨

posts.text:
Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan walked into AI Engineer Singapore last week and demoed the personal AI agent he built for his diplomatic work. Reddit is quite salty about the actual technical implementation, but the key points still stand. Three of them:

1/ Real value gets created at the ground level, not the macro level.

He referenced a point by Neil Lawrence (Cambridge ML professor) that the economic payoff from AI won't come from models or government strategies, it comes when individual professionals adopt it to improve their actual workflows. Department by department, role by role.

There's a lot of noise about which frontier model is better, which AI company did what. But the person who will actually move the needle is the BD manager overwhelmed by leads and tradeshows, or the finance professional drowning in monthly reporting. They know their pain points better than anyone. The moment one of them sees someone in their exact situation saving hours a week, the "I don't have time for this" objection dissolves. When there is enough belief, bandwidth stops being an excuse.

2/ Leaders especially need to get their hands dirty.

"You cannot govern a technology that you have only been briefed on."

Probably the most reshared line from his speech. Ground-level staff and the broader LinkedIn universe will figure out the tech first - job demands will push them there. But AI fundamentally shifts how much a single person can do, and what teams are actually for. Leaders who engage with the topic at length without trying it for themselves - and there are layers of insulation between them and the actual work, so ironically adoption may be slower where it matters most - will find themselves governing, or being governed by, something they don't understand.

3/ The barriers have genuinely collapsed.

He described what he did as "tool assembly", downloading open-source components, connecting them, learning by doing. If a foreign minister with his level of obligations can find the time to experiment and find it worth continuing, there's undoubtedly something there for everyone. All it takes is the willingness to look beyond the day-to-day and just try. The first step leads to the next. Like all new things, you don't have to get it all right at once, but it's more important to keep moving.

Side note: presentation geeks will appreciate that he led with his three conclusions upfront before going into the details. Top-down communication done right.

Link to his keynote below.

A few days ago at AI Engineer SG, Minister Balakrishnan showed off his AI "Second Brain."

A self-hosted agent. Running on a Raspberry Pi. Wired into Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack. Persistent memory. Drafts his briefings, answers his questions, condenses what he reads. He said he doesn't dare switch it off.

It's a tidy concept for a high level world diplomat.

For filmmakers it's slightly stranger.

Our "first brain" already lives across 14 external drives, a Notion that hasn't been opened since 2024, a Frame.io project that expired, three WhatsApp groups full of pegs, and a folder called REFS_FINAL_v3_actuallyfinal. The 2nd brain isn't a fancy new layer for us. It's the layer that was supposed to be there all along.

So at the next FaiGHT CLUB, AI Film Lab is poking at exactly that — at indie filmmaker scale.

The Minister runs his on a Raspberry Pi. We're running ours on the laptops we brought into the room. Hermes Agent, installed locally. Telegram bridge, same as his. One sandboxed skill, end to end, on a Friday night.

Not no-human-in-the-loop. Not a national digital twin. One filmmaker, one agent, one Telegram thread, one honest test.

If "2nd Braining" is going to mean anything for indie content / TV / film work in Singapore, somebody has to waddle in and try it on the ground.

Plus we are super stoked to have Matt Brown from ZeroHours to lead the Hermes Installation this Friday. I have attended their workshop and I have both my OpenClaw and Hermes humming since.

Come waddle.

Singapore's Foreign Minister built his own AI agent.

A second brain for diplomacy.

At AI Engineer yesterday, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan casually walked through how he uses Nanoclaw to think through complex decisions - remembering context, retrieving what matters, surfacing connections he'd otherwise miss.

It hit on exactly what I spoke about on the AI Engineer stage: the Memory Layer for AI agents.

Because a "second brain" isn't about asking better questions.

It's about building systems that: → Remember context → Retrieve what matters → Understand past decisions → Help you think better over time
And that's where AI agents need to go next.

Better models aren't enough. Longer context windows aren't enough. Not if every workflow starts from zero.

The next leap is persistent memory - agents that carry context across tasks, tools, codebases, teams, and decisions.

From stateless code to persistent intelligence.

That's the thesis I'm betting on. And judging by the conversations in the room - with founders, operators, engineers, and fellow alums (met so many fellow YC Alums!) - a lot of serious builders are betting on it too.

Huge kudos to 65labs for assembling one of the most high-signal AI communities in the region.

posts.text:
We live in an era where almost any cognitive task can be outsourced... Except personal understanding and accountability.

I was struck by the recent address from Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, to a room of #AI engineers.

He articulated a principle that ought to be foundational for any leader navigating our current technological landscape:
"We are now at an age where you can outsource a lot of stuff. Calculations, computation, memory, replication, dissemination of knowledge. The one thing which you cannot outsource is your personal understanding." 

Today, we can easily commoditise compute power, data storage, and algorithmic execution. Yet, the strategic foresight and the ethical burden of how these tools are deployed must remain on the shoulders of leadership. 

This is a dynamic we encounter regularly in our work at Homelands AI. Time and again, we find that the most significant barrier to meaningful AI transformation (more so than AI capabilities) is a gap in executive comprehension. 

Rather than merely theorising about the technology, Dr Balakrishnan built his own AI assistant - a 'second brain' designed to manage the immense cognitive load of international diplomacy. 

By assembling open-source tools like #NanoClaw to host Claude-based agents, integrating them with WhatsApp, and running the entire bespoke setup locally on a modest Raspberry Pi computer (a wonderful British innovatino), he created a highly functional system to research topics, draft speeches, and process complex geopolitical data. 

When those who craft our laws and steer our enterprises actually engage with the mechanics of a technology, the entire discourse elevates.

Singapore’s Foreign Minister, Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan, did something highly unusual for a senior politician. He publicly shared the architecture of the AI system he personally built and now uses every day as a “second brain” for diplomacy.

posts.text:
PokeAI Demo- Where Pokemon NPCs finally think and reason back AI Engineer Hackathon Singapore

For those of us who grew up in the 2000s, Pokémon FireRed was not just a game. It was the first rival battle that made you nervous, the first time you asked Professor Oak what to do, the first Pokémon you called your own.

What if the NPCs in that game could actually think?

PokeAI brings that world back and levels it up with AI. The rival walks up, remembers your team, adapts his moves. The professor reads your party before giving advice. The Pokémon you describe gets drawn in FireRed's art style and compiled into the ROM. We did not build a chatbot layered on top of a game. We patched the original FireRed ROM, injected AI hooks into the GBA C source, and connected it live to GPT-5.5. Every AI response appears in the game's native textbox. Every AI decision is written directly into GBA memory.

The first feature is Professor GPT 5.5, an AI NPC scientist in Oak's Lab. Type a question on the GBA naming screen, press OK, and GPT-5.5 answers inside the game's native textbox, encoded in FireRed's proprietary character set and displayed through the original dialog engine. Ask for battle advice and it reads your live party to respond in context. No overlay. No external window. It runs through the game itself.

The second and core feature is an AI rival powered by GPT-5.5. Before the battle in Oak's Lab, GPT reads your live party, the rival's party, and a persistent memory of past encounters it wrote after previous battles. It produces a battle plan: which Pokémon the rival leads with, move priority scores for each of his moves, and an opening taunt delivered in-game. Those scores are written into EWRAM and read by a C hook compiled into the ROM, biasing the native battle AI toward the GPT strategy on every turn. The rival remembers past battles and adapts his strategy across the session.

The stretch feature is a companion website where GPT Image 2 generates FireRed-style pixel-art sprites from a plain text description, with iterative refinement through the image editing API. The generated Pokémon can be connected into the actual game by rebuilding the ROM through our open-source pipeline, poke-ai.

The stack is a patched pret/pokefirered ROM, an mGBA Lua bridge polling EWRAM every frame, a FastAPI Python server, and OpenAI GPT-5.5 and GPT Image 2.

We grew up with this game. We just gave it a mind.

Day 1 at #AIEngineerSingapore.

Sharing a few points from the most operationally dense session of the day:

Beyond RAG: Agentic RAG Workflows
Pierre-Loic Doulcet, LlamaIndex

Techniques to improve the overall quality:

→ Cross-encoder reranking (improves both precision and recall)
→ Query rewriting, HyDE & Multi-query RRF
→ Use Agentic RAG / CRAG instead of regular RAG step
→ Caption-and-index for images (over separate CLIP embeddings)
→ Preserve spatial text, don't flatten multi-column layouts and tables

A few operational principles that stuck:

→ Parsing should be idempotent. Store the raw document so you can re-parse as models or techniques improve.
→ More metadata is good.
→ Use Parse Bench to pick the right parser model
→ Most enterprise data isn't tables but json or structured data, store them separately & route at runtime (Vector DB vs Structured DB store)

Will also try out LiteParse & LlamaParse for parsing.

Came across this talk by Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, at AI Engineer Singapore and found it useful for a slightly different reason. It is not a deeply technical talk. It is a practical story from someone in a leadership role, working in a public and societal context, who is experimenting with AI by applying it to his own work.

One point stated in the talk is - the real value of AI may not only come from large platforms or enterprise-level strategies. It often starts much closer to the work itself: workflow by workflow, team by team, person by person.

It also connects well with Deloitte’s 2026 Global Human Capital Trends report, which makes a similar point from an organisational lens: technology alone is not the differentiator. The value comes from intentional work design, human judgement, adaptability, culture, and how people and machines are brought together in practice.

In both cases, the message is not: buy AI technology and the magic happens - AI becomes valuable when people closest to the work understand the tools, experiment with them, adapt them to their context, and stay accountable for the final judgement.

➡️ One practical starting point for anyone : 
Choose one recurring workflow and map where AI could support preparation, analysis, drafting, decision-making, review, or follow-up — while making clear where human judgement and accountability must remain.

You could also apply this lens more functionally ⤵️: 
For HR: where could AI improve employee experience without weakening trust or fairness?
For product marketers: where could AI help with customer insight, positioning, messaging, or campaign iteration without losing strategic judgement?
For managers: where could AI reduce cognitive overload while improving the quality of decisions?

posts.text: our event is called ai engineer singapore. and at some point while building it, we had to ask ourselves - what does that word even mean anymore? nobody calls themselves an "excel user." it's just a tool. there's no translation layer between you and the outcome - so the identity stays with the domain, not the tool. for a long time, software wasn't like that. if you had domain expertise - in healthcare, education, finance, whatever - you still needed someone to translate your knowledge into a product - that person has a clear identity of an "engineer" that closes that gap. with ai, this is shifting, as more types of people are building alongside each other. at our community hackathons, 50% of finalists were non-traditional engineers - therapists building mental health tools, educators designing adaptive learning systems. designers are shipping code. pms are prototyping in production. non-technical founders are building their own mvps. if you're building and pushing yourself to learn - you belong in these spaces, even if you don't fit the traditional definition of "engineer." this is exactly the shift we designed AI Engineer Singapore around. the technical bar is high - we're not watering anything down. expect laptops open, tools getting tested, and ideas taking shape in real time. but we built this for every type of builder: → software engineers & researchers — deep talks on architecture, infra, and what's working in production → design practitioners — a full track on crafting ai-native product experiences → hardware & robotics builders — foundation models meeting the physical world → founders & product leaders — playbooks for prototyping, shipping and scaling ai products → leaders driving ai transformation — strategy, org design, and making adoption stick → learners & career switchers — exposure to what's possible and a community to build alongside the word we keep coming back to isn't "engineer." it's "builder." and builders come from everywhere. if you see yourself anywhere in that list, come join us may 15-17: https://lnkd.in/gUmMrMsK 🥃 Agrim Singh Rachael De Foe Kaspar Hidayat Ivan Leo # AI Engineer Singapore: Building Beyond Traditional Definitions

posts.text: The best idea I heard at AI Engineer Singapore today wasn't about a model or a framework. It was a question: "Why is this important for the user?" That came from the Airfoil session by Min Kim and Phil Hedayatnia, but it could have been the thesis for the whole day. Almost every talk was, in some way, about the gap between building something impressive and building something that actually works. Exa's conrad soon made the case for owning your full stack when you're building search for agents - not humans. The insight is simple but easy to miss: agents have completely different needs, and most tools weren't designed with that in mind. Optimising for agents only becomes possible when you control the whole pipeline. The same idea showed up in the Mastra demo by Sam Bhagwat. The framework is modular and ships with the primitives you need for agentic use cases. The philosophy behind it is straightforward: to be composable, not clever. ByteDance's Chen Xiaoyu showcased Seedream, Seedance, and the Lumina platform for visual generation workflows. The demos were impressive, but the more striking thing was how production-ready the tooling already feels. The distance between "cool thing in a lab" and "usable in a real workflow" is closing faster than most people expect. Function first, then form. That's easy to say and hard to practice - especially when the technology is genuinely exciting. But if today had a theme, that was it. really cool!

posts.text: how did a non-technical person build apps with thousands of users and raise six figures? the answer is in how i learned. i didn't wait for a nicely packaged curriculum to catch up. i went straight to the people building the tools and learned from them. i live on twitter. i follow the CEOs, founders, and engineers behind cursor, vercel, codex, claude code - the people actually building the tools. and the moment someone drops a demo video, 10 mins and a download later, i've already shipped something with it. posts.text: community events changed my life - which is why i spend nights and weekends outside my startup bringing them to more people. i went to my first ai engineer conference in san francisco, and it was worth every 15 hours of that flight. - i learned about evals from braintrust — a company on the forefront of it — through their hands-on workshop. - i listened to folks from prime intellect break down rlhf and reinforcement learning in a way that actually made sense to me. these weren’t things i could’ve picked up from a blog post or a youtube video alone. and more importantly, i walked out feeling like i belonged in the room, even though i’m not a traditional engineer. that feeling matters more than people realize - i got to learn from incredibly smart ppl who made me feel comfortable asking questions. that experience is exactly why i wanted to bring ai engineer to singapore. some of the best things in this industry come from simply putting people in the same room - giving them surface area to collaborate, discuss, and stumble into ideas together. being around endlessly curious people who want to share what they know and geek out about cutting edge stuff. and this is the part i think gets overlooked. the ecosystems that companies grew out of were built by communities exactly like this. collaborators finding each other. companies being formed. entire industries growing because someone decided to bring people together. none of that shows up in a foot traffic report or a quarterly dashboard. so when companies that benefited from these ecosystems choose to pay it forward and support community, it means the world to us organizers. it keeps the flywheel going: more builders, more energy, more people who get to feel like they belong in the room. that’s the real return. you just have to zoom out far enough to see it. posts.text: We’re officially ONE WEEK OUT from AI Engineer Singapore… and wow, it will be quite the week. We kicked things off yesterday with the AIE Unconference, and it was such a fun reminder of why we do this in the first place. Over 200 people gathered in one room on a Thursday night (!!!) for a night of demos and talks from builders in the community, people sharing the weird, ambitious, experimental things they’ve been thinking about and building. It was also great to see two of my fellow Yale-NUS alums Hrishi Olickel and Minu Choi up there repping liberal arts in the AI space ;) The main conference might be sold out (still wrapping my mind around this, especially cos we've actually got a waitlist!), but this has become so much bigger than just a weekend. If you still want to be part of it, there are plenty of ways to get involved: 1. My friends 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang and Rachael De Foe are sponsoring students who want to attend the conference, out of their own pockets. Spaces like this can be incredibly formative, and we want to make sure more young builders get access to rooms like these. Apply by May 13th: https://lnkd.in/gc6CNahZ 2. We've been joking that the conference has somehow turned into the "Summer of AI", with tons of workshops, meetups, and other side events hosted by teams across the ecosystem. If you’re around, this is honestly one of the best times to be in Singapore as a builder right now: https://www.aievents.sg/ Huge thank you to everyone who’s been part of this so far, our speakers, sponsors, partners, and the community that keeps showing up. And to the team… I still can’t quite believe we’re pulling this off on top of our full-time jobs. This only works because people care that much about building something meaningful for this space. Can’t wait to welcome everyone very, very soon. See you around this week!!! 💫 Ivan Leo Kaspar Hidayat Nehal Agrawal 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan Brian C. So excited! Summerrrrr ☀️ of AI Amazing!

posts.text: I’ll be speaking at AI Engineer Singapore this weekend about how evolutionary algorithms can shape agent behavior, and why the tooling around agents matters as much as the models themselves. As agents move from demos into real software engineering work, the core challenge is no longer just prompting. It is building systems where agent behavior can be represented, varied, measured, selected, and improved. Evolutionary algorithms offer a useful lens for this. Agents can be treated as candidates in a search process. Their tool use, plans, traces, costs, errors, and outcomes become signals. The surrounding infrastructure becomes the fitness environment. This talk will explore that idea through experiments across several tools I’ve built, including codedb for code intelligence, devswarm for parallel agent orchestration, Graff for terminal-first agent workflows, nanobrew for reproducible environments, and other pieces of the agent development stack. Excited to share more this weekend and see you guys there!!! 🥃 Agrim Singh Sherry Jiang 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan Rachael De Foe Ivan Leo So cracked 👑 so excited to have you! The 🐐 appears woohoo lets go!! Exciting! Super cool!!!

posts.text: Making AI accessible is not just about sharing knowledge and skills, but building social capital that opens up future opportunities. Great thoughts by Ainul I cleared my weekend to attend the most coveted AI conference in Singapore. My eczema had other plans. Day 1 of AI Engineer Singapore had me buzzing with ideas as I moved within SMU for workshops I secured weeks in advance. I pushed through in Singapore humidity to learn from the builders actively shipping in this space. I even arranged conversations with speakers I wanted to go deeper with. I unfortunately ended Day 1 with a full-body eczema flare once I returned to my hotel room (which I booked to be much nearer to the event venues). I made the painful decision to “miss” attending Day 2 in person. Fortunately, AI Engineer Singapore had made the main stage talks freely available — a ten-hour livestream, no paywall. So I watched from bed, hours after they aired. But then I started catching up on the LinkedIn notifications I had missed. Students chosen to attend the conference on scholarship tickets were posting their delighted reflections. All of them tagged their sponsors by name, unprompted by the organisers. One of the names was mine. I hadn’t announced it on any platform yet, but I was a personal contributor to the student scholarships when organiser Rachael De Foe shared an invitation to do so. Having been a university student who benefited from scholarships and bursaries, I had seen a chance to give back. Reading the students’ posts had me feeling more present in the room than I was attending the workshops in person on Day 1. Being absent from the room made me realise I’d never fully appreciated what the room was actually for. It’s not just livestreams and recordings that make the AI conversation accessible. It’s the networking and inspiration that happens out of being in the same physical space. The offhand introduction that turns into mentorship and even business opportunities. The ambient credibility of having been there, among the people actively shaping where AI goes next in this region, not merely learning from them. I’m talking about social capital, not just skills and experience. We talk about making AI accessible. We usually mean free tools, open-source models, public livestreams. But accessibility is also: who gets to be in the rooms where relationships are made. Who gets introduced to whom. Who gets the warm referral that opens the next door. The students who tagged me didn’t need my contribution to be capable. They needed one barrier removed so everything they already had could compound. I wasn’t in the room on Day 2. But I was still in the room — because I’d helped put someone else there first. If you’re in a position to do the same — a scholarship, a referral, an open calendar, even a workshop — you don’t have to wait for a formal programme. Build access intentionally. The way you’d design any system worth building. 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang, Kaspar Hidayat, Nehal Agrawal, Gabriel Chua * +1

posts.text: I first met Vivian Balakrishnan as an exchange student of the Singapore International Foundation, in a fellow reception hosted at the Istana. He was Minister of Community Development and Youth at the time, if I remember right, and was already impressive but approachable and down to earth. So it’s super exciting to get a chance to learn from him again - this time as the role model for public servants embracing AI. Looking forward to catching up if you’ll also be at AI Engineer Singapore! We are so incredibly honoured to welcome Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, to the lineup of speakers for AI Engineer Singapore. A few weeks ago, Minister Balakrishnan casually dropped a technical writeup of his personal AI system online. Raspberry Pi. Claude. Local embeddings. Knowledge graphs. A full architecture breakdown. And the global AI community noticed because it reflected something bigger: a willingness to engage with these systems directly, publicly, and practically. To kick off AIE Singapore, Minister Balakrishnan will share his experience experimenting with open-source AI tools and building a “second brain” workflow, alongside broader reflections on how AI may reshape global dynamics, and the way people work, think, and manage information. In a role that demands navigating enormous volumes of information and constant context-switching, his reflections will set the tone for the conference in exactly the way we hoped: That meaningful conversations about AI should not stay abstract. They should involve understanding its parameters through practical engagement with the technology. And that Singapore has become the place where that kind of engagement happens seriously. posts.text: most “ai conferences” are just people narrating the future at you. cool vibes, zero muscle memory. we think that’s backwards. if you leave without having used the tools, broken them a bit, and figured out where they actually hold up - what did you even attend? so we flipped the format at AI Engineer Singapore and as part of the tickets extend a slate of workshops for all attendees. — day 1 (may 15): you don’t watch. you build. the entire first day is workshops. no panels. no passive listening. 60–90 minute sessions where you’re inside the tools, shipping something real, with the teams who built them walking you through it. here’s what’s confirmed so far (more dropping when the portal opens may 1st): ⸻ build with the tools actually rewriting software OpenAI Codex — structure real agent workflows, coordinate subagents, and let codex execute while you steer. this is how it actually gets used in engineering teams. Google Gemini - go from prompt → full-stack app using ai studio + antigravity. frontend, backend, db, deploy - end to end. Cursor - move past autocomplete into agent-first dev. parallel agents, /worktree, /best-of-n, design mode, mcp. run your repo like a factory. MagicPath - turn a sketch, figma frame, or screenshot into production-ready react. compress the entire design → code handoff into one loop. ⸻ agents that actually do things Manus - see how agents become persistent systems: scheduled tasks, event triggers, enterprise controls. less chatbot, more operating system. Mastra - build an agent → turn it into a “claw” (tools, memory, workflows, evals, deploy). prototype to prod, no handwaving. Zo - spin up recurring workflows from plain language. research agents, daily briefings, automations that run while you’re asleep. ⸻ infra for agents that survive reality Arize - trace your agents, turn failures into evals, actually improve behavior. the missing loop most teams skip. Exa - build a research agent with real retrieval: semantic search, live crawl, async deep research with citations. not toy rag. LlamaIndex - go beyond “chat with pdf.” multi-doc reasoning, messy enterprise data, agents that take structured actions. Convex - real-time state + backend that doesn’t fight your agents. systems that don’t fall apart after demo day. PostHog - close the loop: track → decide → act. turn usage into iteration, not dashboards no one reads. ⸻ this is just the initial slate. more sessions are getting finalized and will show up when the portal opens. if you care about actually using this stuff - not just hearing about it - this is the day that matters. bookings open sharp on 1st may. workshop slots are fastest fingers first. 🎟️ ticket link in comments. happy bird pricing ends 1 may. 📅 may 15–17 · capitol kempinski and pullman hotel, singapore Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Kaspar Hidayat Adlin Zainal Ivan Leo This! -> if you leave without having used the tools, broken them a bit, and figured out where they actually hold up - what did you even attend? workshops were some of my favorite parts of aie in sf and nyc! can’t wait to bring them with awesome builders coming from overseas. ok so just so we're clear, i'll be MIA on friday so i can attend these workshops yeah 🙂↔️ getting my laptop ready to learn from other ai teams 🤓 What are the capacities of the workshops? 🚀🚀🚀

posts.text: Community events are why we do what we do. I always wanted to build the community in Singapore I didn’t have when starting out. Step by step we’re getting there :) community events changed my life - which is why i spend nights and weekends outside my startup bringing them to more people. i went to my first ai engineer conference in san francisco, and it was worth every 15 hours of that flight. - i learned about evals from braintrust — a company on the forefront of it — through their hands-on workshop. - i listened to folks from prime intellect break down rlhf and reinforcement learning in a way that actually made sense to me. these weren’t things i could’ve picked up from a blog post or a youtube video alone. and more importantly, i walked out feeling like i belonged in the room, even though i’m not a traditional engineer. that feeling matters more than people realize - i got to learn from incredibly smart ppl who made me feel comfortable asking questions. that experience is exactly why i wanted to bring ai engineer to singapore. some of the best things in this industry come from simply putting people in the same room - giving them surface area to collaborate, discuss, and stumble into ideas together. being around endlessly curious people who want to share what they know and geek out about cutting edge stuff. and this is the part i think gets overlooked. the ecosystems that companies grew out of were built by communities exactly like this. collaborators finding each other. companies being formed. entire industries growing because someone decided to bring people together. none of that shows up in a foot traffic report or a quarterly dashboard. so when companies that benefited from these ecosystems choose to pay it forward and support community, it means the world to us organizers. it keeps the flywheel going: more builders, more energy, more people who get to feel like they belong in the room. that’s the real return. you just have to zoom out far enough to see it.

posts.text: Even after shipping multiple products through vibe coding, there is still so much to learn about this rapidly evolving technology. I was so excited to join the AI coding course run by Sherry and Agrim, who themselves are founders with a passion to build a vibrant AI builder community. It was such a great learning experience, joined by many other people from all walks of life, curious about vibe coding. Many learners started with zero vibe coding experience, and finished building amazing functional apps they can actually use in their daily life in just two days! I myself have learnt a lot about Manus and Cursor, which I’ve not used extensively before. And these are both powerful tools that I would definitely put to use. I really think learning vibe coding is one of the best investments one can make, and now is the right time to do it. If anyone is looking to learn about vibe coding in Singapore. I highly recommend the AI coding course by this power duo. i never set out to be a community person. i'm a builder at heart. for over 10 years i've been obsessed with creating beautiful yet useful product experiences - the kind that make people feel empowered. that's still what i do every day. but while building my own company, i started learning to code with ai. and i started sharing what i was learning online. then something unexpected happened. people didn't just want the content - they wanted to be in the room, building together. that's what started code with ai. then the meetups. then hackathons. and now a full-blown conference - ai engineer, the largest builder-focused ai event - coming to singapore for the first time. and tbh i'm still stunned by the impact: - people finding jobs through connections made at our events - teams that formed at hackathons turning into actual companies - builders in vietnam and malaysia and beyond starting their own hackathons after seeing ours and in hindsight, the gap was always obvious. there are incredibly talented builders in singapore and southeast asia. they just need to be seen. i'm so grateful for my co-organizers who are building ai engineer singapore alongside me. all of us do this on an almost volunteer basis - nights, weekends, on top of our full-time jobs, sometimes putting in our own money to make sure things actually happen. and we do this because we deeply believe that the work happening here deserves a world-class stage. and we're building it. Becky Xia Agree that learning "good" vibe coding and prompt engineering are some of the best investments! It not only helps us build and launch faster, but also changes how we think about many things. So many possibilities ahead!

The shape of the room is what makes this one count — researchers, operators, and founders demoing custom-trained models, emotional intelligence in agents, performant agentic tooling. Real systems that move past chat into execution. Three forces converging on agents in one room: the community actually shipping them, a platform built to run them at scale, and a network that puts them in front of who matters. Each on its own is just a node. Together, during AIE week, it starts to look like infrastructure. None of this happened because anyone pushed for it. People kept showing up. Kept demoing real work. posts.text: You can just do things~ 😃 💯 Proud of this team!! Majulah Singapura 🇸🇬 Where in the world can you find a senior government leader with a personal AI stack published on GitHub? How many would be willing to talk about it in a room full of builders? Which is why we are so incredibly honoured to welcome Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, to the lineup of speakers for AI Engineer Singapore. A few weeks ago, Minister Balakrishnan casually dropped a technical writeup of his personal AI system online. Raspberry Pi. Claude. Local embeddings. Knowledge graphs. A full architecture breakdown. And the global AI community noticed because it reflected something bigger: a willingness to engage with these systems directly, publicly, and practically. To kick off AIE Singapore, Minister Balakrishnan will share his experience experimenting with open-source AI tools and building a “second brain” workflow, alongside broader reflections on how AI may reshape global dynamics, and the way people work, think, and manage information. In a role that demands navigating enormous volumes of information and constant context-switching, his reflections will set the tone for the conference in exactly the way we hoped: That meaningful conversations about AI should not stay abstract. They should involve understanding its parameters through practical engagement with the technology. And that Singapore has become the place where that kind of engagement happens seriously. 🥃 Agrim SinghSherry JiangAdlin ZainalNehal AgrawalBrian C.🇸🇬 Yong Quan TanIvan LeoKaspar Hidayat majulah indeeeeeeeed

posts.text: I can’t believe a coding tool just saved me hours planning a conference trip. I’m going to AI Engineer Singapore next week, and the usual conference prep mess started immediately. Flights in Gmail. Bookings in Gmail. Calendar blocks. Satellite events on Luma. Open attendee lists. People I should probably meet. Places to work from. Gym options. A few things I need to buy before the event. Normally this becomes 14 browser tabs and a messy note. This time I gave it to Codex. The workflow was simple: 1. Build a personal conference CRM I checked Luma events with public participant lists, collected LinkedIn profiles, then had Codex qualify who I should meet based on relevance, overlap, and where we could create value for each other. Much better than randomly showing up and hoping for good conversations. 2. Arrange the logistics Codex checked flight and booking confirmations in Gmail, reviewed my calendar, found workout options before the conference, suggested places in Singapore worth visiting, and grouped everything by area so I’m not crossing the city five times a day. 3. Turn it into a plan Calendar updated. Commutes checked. Shopping mall found. Events mapped. Priority people listed. Open loops visible. This took around one hour. The funny part is that I use the same tool for macOS apps, web apps, client projects, research, and content. And now it also helps organize life. I think this is the underrated part of agents. They are becoming a general execution layer around messy context. You still need judgment. You need to define the outcome, give access to the right tools, and check the work. But the gap between “I should probably organize this” and “it is organized” is getting much smaller. # Codex Saves Hours Planning Conference Trip with AI

posts.text: "i'm not really an AI engineer." the civil servant who said this to me a few weeks ago had just spent the conversation describing software he'd built. internal tools. real stack. real tradeoffs. saving his team hours every week. using the same gotchas i hit at my startup. he wasn't being modest. he genuinely didn't think he counted. he's wrong. and he's not alone. i keep meeting people like him. marketers, PMs, designers, domain experts shipping things their companies couldn't have built two years ago, all quietly convinced they're not real engineers because they don't have the credential. the definition changed underneath them. most haven't noticed yet. i wrote a piece about why. it covers: - why every AI skeptic you respected quietly flipped in late 2025 - why the "AI engineer" title has fractured into five roles with different pay bands - why evaluation, not prompting, is the highest-leverage skill of this era - why democratizing creation without democratizing judgment is dangerous my bet: within two years, "AI engineer" as a title will be dead. not because the work disappears but because it becomes the default. like "internet engineer" before it. if you've been shipping with AI and quietly wondering whether you count, you probably do. this is also why we're running AI Engineer Singapore, May 15–17 at Capitol Kempinski - the first AI engineer conference in Asia - so people get access to the latest know-how in the space and hear from the people making it happen. if you've been building with AI, this is the room you want to be in. full piece linked here ↓ Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Kaspar Hidayat Adlin Zainal Ivan Leo we're all BUILDERS now creating a future together that we're all proud of :) It's a great piece but wouldn't want to coin the term 'Dead' for an AI engineer, there's still high demand for them in the enterprise fields, it would seem that their roles will evolve and advance further similar to all engineering roles we have seen in the past 10 years ai engineers, everywhereeeee! 🙌🇸🇬

posts.text: Why the #HackathonHangover is where the real innovation happens. Most hackathons end at the final buzzer. But for me, the real work continues on as agentic processes become more prevalent across multiple industries. Especially one I used to belong to: advertising and commercial content production. Despite me looking poofy in the face [maybe a bad camera angle or just maybe how I look in real life], here is the video on the project we did at the 65labs AI Engineer #Hackathon at National University of Singapore, I built VibeDirector as part of my ongoing work with UNITY OS Eve Count. Because of a last-minute gear pivot, I had to ship "lite"—architecting a mobile-first PWA on a Chromebook. It was a day of friction, manual Git uploads, and limited energy. But it forced a realization: The future of content isn't about better tools; it's about better Orchestration. What is VibeDirector? It’s an agentic creative studio that acts as a conductor and the future of most online content workflows. The Intent: I speak to Gemini 3.1 Flash-Live in real-time. The Brain: Adaption Labs acts as the execution layer, managing the task-chain. The Output: It autonomously triggers Lyria (audio) and Veo 3 (video) to render a synchronized cinematic "vibe" in seconds. This is all very different from the content workflows we used to do; where there were pre-production meetings, script revisions, talent and location, gear and crew call sheets, the actual shoot day and then, post production. We have come far from that model, which is still relevant, but as we go deeper into agentic processes, the new roles for my counterparts in the applied arts should also evolve. In the near future, we won't spend hours in timelines; we will use voice-first agents to orchestrate entire media stacks. Content creation is shifting from crafting to conducting, and I truly believe those who were always creators, will always be builders. Huge thanks to 65labs for the pressure cooker environment that forced this pivot. VibeDirector started as a hack, but it’s becoming a vision for how we go beyond just documents, to both visual and audio media. #AI #AgenticWorkflows #VibeDirector #65labs #FutureOfContent #GeminiAI #Multimodal

posts.text: Most AI events have slides. This one has laptops open. On 7 May, 150 of us pile into Stripe Singapore. The hosts demo first — an agent doing real work, a RAG system over a real corpus, evals catching a real bug. Then the room takes over: anonymous question board, vote up what you want answered most. Whatever wins, we open the laptop and show you. Real APIs, real bugs, real trade-offs. "How do I evaluate an agent?" — we write the eval live. Then six AIE speakers — Minu, Hrishi, Suveen, Justin, Rach, Jed — walk through what they're actually shipping. Short, punchy, in the wild. What broke, what they wish they'd known on day one. No keynote stage. No 500-person ballroom. No spectator seats. We chose this format because of what every event we've run has taught us: people remember the rooms they participated in, not the ones they watched. We wanted attendees to walk out with the felt experience of being an AI engineer — not adjacent to the work, inside it. That all six speakers are based here isn't a logistics decision.
