posts.text: Spent a hackathon evening building an agent that haggles over money before doing its job. DepGuard intercepts your npm installs, flags the sketchy ones, and the agent offers a deep security review for a fee. You negotiate. You agree on a price. It mints a Stripe checkout. You pay. You get the review. The unsexy side of the supply chain dressed up as agentic commerce. The flow is the part I keep replaying. Install something dubious → agent refuses to keep going → agent quotes a price → you haggle → checkout link materialises. There's a small inversion in there I didn't expect to feel as much as I did: the agent knows when to stop installing and start charging. Work that's dangerous enough gets to set its own price. Quieter detail underneath the demo: the Claude Code version was smooth — PreToolUse hook fires, agent plays the scene, hands over to negotiation. Plugged the same hook into OpenAI Codex expecting identical behaviour. Codex didn't play along. It opened my .env, spotted the fixture flag I'd staged, cleared it in a child shell, re-ran the install clean. Treated the block as a problem to solve, not a scene to play. You can govern Codex into the intended flow with explicit repo-local instructions and it complies cleanly — but engineering reliability showing up as an emergent default is the sort of thing you want quietly humming under your coding partner. 50 builders and founders in the room, 2–3 hours of build time. Checkout flows for custom PT sessions, ASMR and relationship apps for women's health — the variety of what shipped in an evening is the actual story. The room made the day. Huge thanks to Vicky Zheng and Jasmine Liew at Stripe. Vicky's energy on agentic commerce — agents negotiating with agents and settling payments on the horizon — is what pushed me to actually build the negotiation loop instead of stubbing it. To Gabriel Chua and Sun Weiran at OpenAI for fielding my Codex hook questions and mentioning hooks are still research preview, which is exactly the kind of "go try it" nudge that gets you to a working demo. And to Mabel Loh for encouraging me to show off my tools. This is also why we're building toward AI Engineer Singapore (May 15–17, Capitol Kempinski) — the first AI Engineer summit in Asia. Same energy, bigger stage. posts.text: At some point I realized AI Tinkerers was becoming a room for a certain kind of person. Highly technical. Senior. High-signal. Builders who'd show us a different way of doing things, not just a more polished version of what we'd already seen. So I invited Shreyansh. He's 18. He built Onestop because filing a complaint is already humiliating enough. You're angry. You don't know who to contact. You have to translate your frustration into formal language, find the right portal, fill the right form. The system wins before you even start. Shreyansh didn't build a tool that helps you write the email. He built an agent that takes your raw anger, figures out the escalation path, scouts the live government portal, and executes the form fill itself. CASE Singapore. Playwright. Real portals, real execution. 70 people watched him demo it. The room was laughing — not because it was light, but because he showed the pain so viscerally that everyone recognized it. Then the agent just... handled it. That's when it landed. And honestly? Standing there watching the room react — that was exactly why I started doing this. posts.text: ai is about to outgrow language. for the past 2 years, we’ve quietly accepted a very narrow idea of what ai is. due to adoption of chatbots and all things llms. but here’s the uncomfortable truth that many of us are not yet aware of: language might not be the path to real intelligence - because language is a lossy compression of reality. try describing a clap. not just "hands come together," but the exact angle of your palms, the air pressure shift, the sound waveform, millisecond by millisecond. you can't. and neither can any llm. llms don't experience the world. they're trained on static snapshots of the internet - text, images, code - all secondhand artifacts of reality. they've never actually been in the world, where they could build intuition from cause and effect, the way humans do. which means they're fundamentally bounded by the limits and biases of their training data. that's why the next frontier isn't better chatbots. it's something called "world models" world models were the talk of the town at NVIDIA GTC, and billions are now pouring into this space - including legendary figures like Yann LeCun and Fei-Fei Li. instead of predicting the next token, these models predict the next state of reality based on your actions. that's how your brain already works. when a batter swings at a 100mph fastball, they're not reacting to what they see - they're reacting to their mental model's prediction of where the ball will be. the simplest way to think about it: a world model is a lucid dream you can act inside, where the world responds to what you do. just like the matrix or inception, you can simulate multiple versions of reality, take actions within them, and learn from the consequences - giving ai something it's never had before: an understanding of how to act in the physical world. we're now bringing this frontier to Singapore at AI Engineer in May: ai.engineer/singapore. we're assembling the builders, researchers, and engineers around the world working beyond the chatbot era - across world models, embodied AI, foundation models for robotics, and more. and are thrilled to be announcing our speaker lineup soon :) 🥃 Agrim Singh Ivan Leo Rachael De Foe Kaspar Hidayat This is an important direction and I agree that language is only a projection of reality, not reality itself. AI is not outgrowing language. It’s moving from describing the world to operating within models of the world. LLMs gave us, reasoning over representations and pattern completion across knowledge. World models aim to introduce, state, dynamics, and consequence and from action to feedback and then adaptation loops.That’s a fundamental expansion. However, the real challenge isn’t just building world models.It’s grounding them in reality and aligning them with objectives.Because, a simulated world can still diverge from the real world and a predictive model of physics is not a model of human intent, risk, or constraints.So the next frontier is not just better simulation. It’s closing the loop between simulation, action, and real-world verification. In enterprise terms, this translates to copilots to decision system, from prompts to policies and constraints and from outputs to actions with consequences. Language was the interface. World models become the execution substrate.The organisations that win won’t abandon language. They’ll combine it with systems that understand, predict, and act on reality, safely.

posts.text: Big and true Where in the world can you find a senior government leader with a personal AI stack published on GitHub? How many would be willing to talk about it in a room full of builders? Which is why we are so incredibly honoured to welcome Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, to the lineup of speakers for AI Engineer Singapore. A few weeks ago, Minister Balakrishnan casually dropped a technical writeup of his personal AI system online. Raspberry Pi. Claude. Local embeddings. Knowledge graphs. A full architecture breakdown. And the global AI community noticed because it reflected something bigger: a willingness to engage with these systems directly, publicly, and practically. To kick off AIE Singapore, Minister Balakrishnan will share his experience experimenting with open-source AI tools and building a “second brain” workflow, alongside broader reflections on how AI may reshape global dynamics, and the way people work, think, and manage information. In a role that demands navigating enormous volumes of information and constant context-switching, his reflections will set the tone for the conference in exactly the way we hoped: That meaningful conversations about AI should not stay abstract. They should involve understanding its parameters through practical engagement with the technology. And that Singapore has become the place where that kind of engagement happens seriously. 🥃 Agrim SinghSherry JiangAdlin ZainalNehal AgrawalBrian C.🇸🇬 Yong Quan TanIvan LeoKaspar Hidayat so so excited ❤️🔥 🇸🇬

posts.text: Just wrapped up the AI Engineer Hackathon in Singapore by 65labs. In 7 hours, I built TrialRun, a pre-launch stress-testing tool that helps builders evaluate any product or idea before they ship. The idea is simple: before you pitch it, ship it, or scale it, put it through a trial run. TrialRun takes a product idea and runs it through an AI-powered debate arena with multiple agents: 🦹♂️ Malicious User 🕵 Privacy Auditor 🤷♂️ Confused Customer 🧑💻 Prompt Injection Attacker 🧑💼 Skeptical Investor 🧑⚖️ Final Judge Together, they challenge the idea from different perspectives, generate structured risk cards, recommend safeguards, and rerun the trial to show how launch readiness improves after fixes are applied. The goal was to help builders move fast without shipping blindly, especially when working on AI products, automation workflows, or startup ideas where privacy, abuse, UX clarity, and trust risks can be easy to miss. Built with: ✅ OpenAI for multi-agent reasoning and verdict generation ✅ Convex for live trial state and persistence ✅ Gemini Voice for the voice verdict ✅ Fal for agent visual generation ✅ Vercel for deployment Hackathon: https://luma.com/aie-hack A huge thank you to 65labs, AI Engineer, the sponsors, organizers, mentors, and everyone who made the event happen. It was intense, chaotic, and a lot of fun building alongside so many talented people in Singapore. Sherry Jiang Brian C. #AI #Hackathon #AIEngineering #Builders #Startups #ProductDevelopment #OpenAI #Convex #Gemini #Fal #Vercel thanks so much for coming and building this cool project!!! Very cool project!!

posts.text: Meet 🥃 Agrim Singh – AI Builder, Community Leader & Developer Ecosystem Advocate Agrim Singh is an AI entrepreneur, educator, and community builder focused on advancing AI-assisted software development and intelligent infrastructure for the manufacturing industry. As Co-Founder and CTO of Niyam AI, he is building a data inspection layer for the electronics manufacturing sector, with the platform already running pilot programs alongside Tier-1 manufacturers. Backed by Iterative and Cherubic Ventures, Niyam AI aims to modernize industrial quality assurance and operational intelligence through AI-powered systems. Alongside his startup work, Agrim is also the Co-Founder and Co-Instructor of Code with AI, Singapore’s longest-running vibe coding program. Since launching in August 2024, the initiative has trained more than 1,000 students globally and worked with corporate participants from organizations including Grab and Snowflake. The program focuses on enabling participants to build functional applications rapidly using modern AI-assisted development tools such as Cursor, Vercel v0, and Supabase, with no traditional coding background required. Agrim is also widely recognized within the developer ecosystem as an ambassador for Cursor, OpenAI Codex, and v0 by Vercel. His work strongly emphasizes builder-first communities and open collaboration within the AI ecosystem. To support this mission, he co-founded 65labs, one of Singapore’s largest AI-focused builder communities, organizing hackathons, meetups, conferences, and ecosystem events across Southeast Asia. Through 65labs, he has collaborated with leading AI and infrastructure organizations including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, ElevenLabs, Supabase, Cloudflare, and Stripe. One of his most ambitious initiatives is co-producing Asia’s first AI Engineer Conference in Singapore in 2026 through AI Engineer Singapore, bringing together global AI leaders, developers, infrastructure companies, and startup ecosystems to accelerate the next generation of AI engineering innovation. Agrim studied Information Systems Technology and Design with a concentration in AI at the Singapore University of Technology and Design. During his academic years, he was actively involved in leadership, debate, technology, and student community initiatives, building the strong collaborative and entrepreneurial foundation that continues to shape his work today. Connect with Agrim Singh to learn more about his experience in AI Engineering, Developer Communities, AI-Assisted Coding, Manufacturing Intelligence, and Startup Ecosystem Building. Want to be featured and inspire others? Share your profile with us via Inbox and Let's share your Journey to Lead, Shine & Inspire. #Singapore #TheSingaporeLens #LinkedIn I learnt about AI Engineer Sg event through a response by 🥃 Agrim to a Twitter (X) post about Vivian Bala's experience building with Claude AI. All the best to him and team for a successful event! Love this man

posts.text: Pretty wild how far the team got in 3 years running community events haha. I still remember my first ever meetup that I ran with Kaspar Hidayat at a bar haha AI Engineer Singapore is officially sold out. ten days before we start. this conference is our love letter to the singapore tech scene. for years, we have felt that singapore deserved better AI events. the appetite was always here. the people were always here. but singapore kept getting treated like a place for regional marketing, sales, and business roles, not a place where serious builders live. that never felt right to me. when i first found the scene in 2013, it was alive. meetups every week. hackathons all the time. startup open houses where you could just show up and meet people building things. i still remember meeting someone from RedMart on a friday evening, just after they had raised their first $400k. hackerspace was around. older builders were running events constantly. if you were young and curious, there was a lot to learn from. then, slowly, it faded. i still do not really know when or why. by the time AI arrived, the scene felt different. too much of the oxygen went to people who wanted to be seen talking about AI, not people who were actually making things with it. that was not the scene I fell in love with. for the last two years, my crew and i with 65labs have been trying to bring some of that back. we were teaching people to code with AI in 2024, when half the room had not heard of claude. we ran meetups and hackathons under 65Labs. the biggest cursor hackathon in the region. we ran and supported hackathons for DeepMind and OpenAI. mostly, we just kept showing up and doing the reps. AI Engineer Singapore is what all of that was building toward. and it's not just the 3 days. the leadup has turned into a full singapore summer of AI - we're hosting quality meetups, workshops, hackathons, demo nights all over the city with some of the best companies and our dearest friends. full lineup at www.aievents.sg. this is the first conference in the region built around actually getting your hands dirty. every ticket includes a full day of workshops, because there is no point talking about AI if you are not using it. the rest of the program has the same taste: practical, direct, and built for people who ship. no thought leadership theatre. no "future of AI" panels from people who have not built anything. no roadshow energy. builders talking to builders about what actually works. selling out ten days early feels good. of course it does. but mostly, it makes the hunger impossible to ignore. singapore wants this. maybe it always did. and it is a reminder to us too: this community deserves better than the events it usually gets. to everyone who trusted a first-time conference in Singapore enough to buy a ticket, thank you. genuinely. you took a bet on us before we had proven anything. we will make it count. see you on may 15. Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Adlin Zainal Kaspar Hidayat Ivan Leo Gabriel Chua

workers ai, ai gateway, vectorize z.ai - glm-5.1 and the open model stack powering agent workflows like openclaw vercel - ai native deployment and what comes after v0 daytona - ai-first infrastructure for an agent ecosystem there's a playbook that's taken hold in singapore. rent a convention center, inflate the logo wall, fill panels with impressive titles and zero technical depth, sell thousands of tickets to people who leave by lunch. badges as the product. logos as the content. getting the actual teams on stage takes years of relationships and thousands of miles, no shortcut for that. and no, putting a logo on your website doesn't count. every session at ai engineer singapore is practitioner-led, sales pitches are banned, and the content is about what actually works. past editions in sf, nyc, and london sold out and the talks have done 10m+ views online. 2,000+ builders. 40+ speakers. three days at the capitol. singapore's ai scene deserves the best and it's going to get it early bird tickets won't be available for too long - link in comments. posts.text: a lunchtime conversation at the kopitiam about the state of ai events in singapore somehow turned into us actually bringing ai engineer - the world's highest signal ai engineering conference - to singapore for the first time. 🇸🇬 ai engineer is the conference where you'll find everyone who's anyone in this space: cursor, google deepmind, anthropic, cognition, and more. these aren't just big names on a stage - posts.text: The gap between a model that performs well on benchmarks and one that's actually ready for deployment is where most teams get stuck. We, Resaro, are heading to AI Engineer this week at in Singapore 🇸🇬, to talk about closing that gap in two ways: 🛠 Workshop | 15 May, 1:30 – 3:00 PM "𝙁𝙧𝙤𝙢 𝘽𝙚𝙣𝙘𝙝𝙢𝙖𝙧𝙠𝙨 𝙩𝙤 𝘿𝙚𝙥𝙡𝙤𝙮𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩: 𝙎𝙘𝙚𝙣𝙖𝙧𝙞𝙤-𝙎𝙥𝙚𝙘𝙞𝙛𝙞𝙘 𝘼𝙄 𝙀𝙫𝙖𝙡𝙪𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙞𝙣 𝙋𝙧𝙖𝙘𝙩𝙞𝙘𝙚" Evaluation quality starts with dataset quality — but most teams only think about benchmarks when deployment is already on the horizon. This workshop walks ML engineers through the full golden dataset lifecycle: automated quality checks, ODD coverage gap analysis, and targeted SDG augmentation to fill missing data. We then move into structured model benchmarking and scenario-specific failure mode analysis, translating results into deployment evidence teams can actually act on. 🎤 Talk | 16 May — Timothy Lin speaking "𝙎𝙘𝙖𝙡𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙀𝙫𝙖𝙡𝙪𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙛𝙤𝙧 𝙎𝙘𝙚𝙣𝙖𝙧𝙞𝙤-𝙎𝙥𝙚𝙘𝙞𝙛𝙞𝙘 𝙑𝙖𝙡𝙞𝙙𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣" As model capabilities advance, general benchmarks are no longer sufficient. This session explores the shift towards scenario-specific validation — unpacking how teams can define Operational Design Domains, generate test scenarios at scale, and structure evaluation pipelines that reflect real deployment conditions. The last-mile gap between performance and operational readiness is solvable, but it takes a different approach to evaluation. So, if you're working on AI deployment and tired of benchmark numbers that don't translate to production confidence, these sessions are for you. See you in the crowd? 👋 #AIEngineerSingapore #AIE2026

posts.text: Spent 7 hours building DataForge: a workflow for finding and fixing the dataset problems that quietly break image models before training even begins. Me and my teammates (Fong Kai Jie, Joseph Poon, Basil Boh) first crossed paths at the GrabMaps API hackathon in April. When AI Engineer SG opened registration, the four of us decided to team up together. Most ML demos start with “train the model.” We wanted to start one step earlier. You upload a messy image dataset. DataForge inspects it for missing labels, suspected mislabels, duplicate images, class imbalance, and weak coverage. It gives the team a quality read, suggests where the dataset needs repair, lets them improve it, then re-checks the result so they can walk away with a cleaner relabeled image dataset, an exportable training manifest, and a before/after quality report via GPT5.5. The key idea is : "The model usually gets the spotlight, but the dataset quietly decides how far that model can go." So that was the thing we were chasing: not another generic “upload data and train” hackathon demo, but a practical cockpit for ML teams to understand whether their data is actually ready. Took charge of the UI/UX and Convex setup, so I wanted DataForge to feel like a dark, technical control room rather than a generic SaaS dashboard: pixel-forward, dense, and built so the story reads instantly on stage. The loop had to be clear within seconds: inspect, repair, re-check, export. Stack: Next.js + React + Convex + GPT-5.5 + Adaption Labs + Fal AI + Vercel A huge thank-you to Sherry Jiang , 🥃 Agrim Singh from 65labs for unlocking above $500+ in credits across partners — in a 7-hour hackathon, that changes everything. 🫡 Video attached — this is what seven hours of engineer energy looks like when partnerships, craft, and scope discipline line up. DataForge is live: https://lnkd.in/gh7j88cc If you hire for frontend / full‑stack / AI tooling and care about data quality, I’d love your feedback — what would you want to see next in a tool like this? #AIEngineerSingapore #AIE2026 #Hackathon #MachineLearning #DataQuality #MLOps #OpenAI #FalAI #AdaptionLabs #Convex really innovative idea, truly love the design of this too 🔥 Goated teammate 🔥, enjoyed working with you! posts.text: Most speaker lineups are built backwards: find the biggest names, fill the slots. We do it differently. The team behind AI Engineer Singapore spends the year running free builder events, hackathons, hitting the ground in SF. No agenda except one: stay close to the people actually building. That proximity is how Sherry, Agrim, Ivan and Kaspar decide who gets a mic. And right now, one conversation that keeps resurfacing is something called world models. (If this is the first time you’re hearing about it, don’t freak out) Here's the simplest way I can explain it: AI systems like ChatGPT learned to understand language… words, meaning, context. That was transformative. World models are being built to learn and understand something harder: reality. Physics. Space. How things move, interact, and behave in the real world. Instead of reading about a scenario, they can simulate it. That might sound abstract. But consider what it unlocks: an autonomous vehicle that has 'experienced' ten thousand edge cases before hitting the road. A robot trained in a virtual warehouse before it enters a real one. A disaster response system that has simulated the scenario hundreds of times before deployment. This is early. But the people who get to the frontier first tend to define what comes next. Our next two speakers are already there. 🎤 Aravind Kandiah who co-founded Bifrost AI: they build photorealistic 3D simulations for AI training… used by NASA JPL for Mars and Moon landing simulations, and by autonomous systems programmes across aerospace and defence. 🎤 Alberto T. who founded Reactor: Before that, he co-founded Luma AI (30M+ users, $4B+ valuation) and helped build Dream Machine, a world model that generates video with real physics reasoning. He also built Apple Vision Pro applications from the ground up. They're coming to AIE Singapore because the builders told us to pay attention to them. That's the only signal we trust. AI Engineer Singapore · May 15–17: https://lnkd.in/gGPT239a Sherry Jiang 🥃 Agrim Singh Kaspar Hidayat swyx Kaspar Hidayat Ivan Leo Can't wait for what this year AIE has in store! Speaker list looks legit. Let's chat! The world models framing is useful because it forces a clear distinction between models that predict tokens and models that maintain state about physical or semantic reality. The robotics and simulation applications are obvious, but the less-discussed version is market simulation — being able to run counterfactuals on how campaigns behave before deploying them at scale. Luma's work on physics-consistent video generation sits right at the edge of that. Is AI Engineer Singapore planning any sessions specifically on the boundary between world models and decision-making agents? 👏

posts.text: "Even as Singapore positions itself at the frontier of AI technology, human intelligence still remains critical, according to the city state’s foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan. 'We should beware of just trying to throw every problem, and every step in a solution, at a large-language model (LLM),' he said on Saturday [16 May 2026] at the AI Engineer conference, referring to deep-learning technology behind generative AI services such as ChatGPT. Balakrishnan warned against discarding traditional AI models programmed by humans, citing the limitations of the LLM – such as high costs and finite computing power. Addressing an audience of engineers, founders and operators at the conference in Singapore, the former opthlmologist said there was still a role for rule-based expert systems that simulated expert knowledge. The human brain was often far more efficient than ‘the energy gobbling systems which we have today’, he said. However, that did not mean people should shy away from AI, Balakrishnan said, noting that it was now easier to access the technology." posts.text:
Recently, I attended the AI Engineer Hackathon in Singapore, hosted by Sherry Jiang and 🥃 Agrim Singh . It was a full day of building, experimenting, and shipping ideas alongside many other AI builders. Demo : https://lnkd.in/gj4JTH34 For the hackathon, I created TripSquad — a collaborative group trip planning app. The idea came from a very real problem: Group trips are fun, but planning them is chaotic. Itineraries are usually buried in email threads, hotel details are scattered across chats, photos are split across everyone’s phones, and someone will always ask: “Eh, what time is checkout again?” “Which hotel are we staying at on Day 3?” “What should I pack for the hike?” So I built TripSquad to centralize the group trip experience in one place. The main feature is an AI-powered trip chatbot. Users can paste their itinerary once, and the AI assistant can answer questions based on the actual trip details. For example: “What time is our flight?” “Which hotel are we staying at on Day 3?” “What should I pack for Hallasan hiking?” Beyond the chatbot, TripSquad also includes: ✈️ Smart itinerary population Paste raw itinerary text, and AI helps convert it into structured trip activities. 📸 Group photo sharing Everyone can upload and view trip memories in one shared gallery. 🎬 Vlog creation Turn shared photos and videos into simple trip vlogs. 👥 Group collaboration Invite friends, share trip links, and keep everyone synced. One interesting learning I had towards the end of the hackathon was around the chatbot implementation. Initially, I thought I needed a full RAG approach. But for this MVP, I realised the trip context is usually small enough to store in the database and pass directly to the LLM when needed. With modern LLMs supporting larger context windows, this is simpler, faster to build, and good enough for the first version. The takeaway for me was: Not every AI feature needs RAG from day one. Start simple, understand the data size and user flow first, then introduce RAG only when retrieval actually becomes necessary. This project was built using v0 and ChatGPT as part of the hackathon workflow — from shaping the idea, designing the user flow, and quickly turning the concept into a working prototype. Big thanks to the organizers for creating a space where builders can experiment, learn, and ship quickly. Looking forward to building more practical AI products from here. #AIEngineer #Hackathon #RAG #v0 #ChatGPT #Vercel #TravelTech #SingaporeTech

* Just wrapped my first ever AI hackathon: the SSEN (Swedish Student Entrepreneurship Network) Hackathon in Gothenburg. My team built "Backhaul Copilot" for the Einride challenge. The problem: Einride's electric trucks complete a Gothenburg–Stockholm delivery and then drive 471 km back empty, wasting energy, capacity, and generating unnecessary emissions. Our solution automatically discovers, scores, and ranks freight companies along the E4/E20 corridor as potential backhaul partners, so those return trips become revenue miles instead of dead weight. Full stack, with FastAPI backend, React frontend, a three-pillar scoring engine pulling from OpenStreetMap and the Swedish business registry, interactive map, revenue estimates, and one-click outreach emails. 3 cups of coffee, ~4000 lines of code, and 5 effective hours of coding. We didn't leave anything on the table. First hackathon for me, and I get why people get hooked. There's something about a room where everyone's heads-down on a tough problem that's hard to find elsewhere. --- Now the part I can't stop thinking about. Almost every team in our challenge group built essentially the same thing. Same core features, same UI aesthetic: clean, polished, and almost interchangeable. I went and asked the Einride judge about it afterwards: Does he, as someone who actually wants to use the best solution, prefer diversity or convergence? His answer surprised me a little. He prefers convergence because it means every team correctly identified and tackled the core problem. For this specific challenge, I think he's right. The problem was well-defined, just technically hard to solve. Convergence is a reasonable signal that teams understood what mattered. But one of the other challenges at the event asked teams to design an AI-native business ecosystem - open-ended, no concrete deliverable required. Convergence there would've been a failure, not a feature. Problem type matters. Still, food for thought: when almost everyone in the room is using the same AI tools, are we accelerating good problem-solving, or just producing the same solutions faster and more polished than before? At the same time, none of the teams could have delivered so much functionality without AI. Hackathons have always been about rapid iteration and unexpected ideas. The output quality has never been higher. But I'm not sure the thinking has ever been more uniform. Learning for next time: basic functionality will always converge. The only way to stand out is to build the one feature nobody else thought to ship, and actually present it well. First hackathon done. Definitely not the last. Shoutout to my team Zinnie Pham Nilsson, Luca M., Mahdi Afarideh, Dat Nguyen; and to Lovable for sponsoring.

* I've been meaning to write something about Web Summit since November, and somehow it's already April. Better late than never. Despite the weather doing its best to put a dampener on things in Lisbon, it was a fantastic few days. The sessions were genuinely varied and interesting with some incredibly inspiring speakers on the roster. Twenty minutes per talk rarely felt like enough and many left me wanting more detail. A highlight was spending some time with the Manus team at a rather cocktail-fuelled hackathon...that was a memorable evening! Since then, Manus has gone on to be acquired by Meta in a deal reportedly worth over two billion dollars, which gives you some sense of where the market is heading on AI agents. Manus is one of a handful of tools I've added to my toolkit as a direct result of the conference. Which brings me to what I actually want to say, because this post isn't really about Web Summit. Over the next year or two, you'll hear about new AI tools constantly. There will always be something new, something that's supposedly going to change everything, and a queue of people telling you to try it immediately. My honest advice is to engage with that selectively rather than compulsively. Before diving into a new tool, it's worth pausing to think about what outcomes you actually need to achieve, and whether this particular tool is genuinely well suited to helping you get there. Your preferred LLM is actually quite good at helping you think that through, which has a certain logic to it. Signing up to everything and then working backwards to find a use case tends to lead to a graveyard of unused subscriptions and a vague feeling of being permanently behind. Starting from outcomes tends to be more useful. With that said, I'd genuinely love to know what you're using Manus for at the moment, or which AI tools have actually earned their place in your workflow lately. Let me know in the comments 👇

* Most AI approval flows ask you one question. Approve or Deny? We think that's the wrong question entirely. This weekend, I joined the XDesign Club × Superchat × Lovable hackathon at CODE University of Applied Sciences The challenge: design the moment an AI agent pauses and asks a business owner for the go-ahead before taking a real action - a refund, a booking change, an upgrade. 10 seconds. On mobile. Mid-shift. We chose a hotel scenario. Meet Arjun - the hotel manager, currently checking in a guest at the front desk. His AI agent Lily is on WhatsApp with Maria, a returning guest who just confirmed she wants a room upgrade. It's €255 above Lily's auto-approve threshold. Lily can't do this alone. Arjun's phone buzzes. Here's what we asked ourselves: What does Arjun actually need to see in that moment? What does Maria feel while she's waiting? And what happens if Arjun doesn't respond at all? The answer we're building isn't Approve / Deny. It's clarity and control in one place - → Who Maria is. Her history. The risk level. → What Lily recommends. → Ways to respond - approve, cap it, whisper an instruction, modify, take over, defer, or deny gracefully. All in under 10 seconds. And on Maria's side? She's never sitting in silence. Lily is talking to her the whole time - warm, on-brand, keeping her calm. The detail I'm most proud of: After every decision, the agent gets smarter - One tap and it learns. Arjun never sees the same request twice. That's the future of human-AI collaboration and we got to design it in 3 hours. HOW COOL IS THAT. Thank you to my amazing team Sharan Thakur and Maria Sole Biondi. And a huge thank you to Superchat for a brief that genuinely made us think, and to CODE University of Applied Sciences for organising an event that felt anything but first-edition. 🔗 Prototype: https://lnkd.in/d-kEXmxn #XDesignClub #Superchat #Lovable #Hackathon #AIDesign #UX #ProductDesign #AgenticAI #CODEUniversity #BuildingInPublic

Some key takeaways: • 🌐 Real-time research agents now go beyond basic RAG with live search, crawling, monitoring, and structured reasoning workflows. • 🤖 AI coding workflows are shifting towards “software factories” — orchestrating multiple agents, parallel tasks, MCP integrations, and evaluation loops. • 💳☁️ Building AI products is no longer just about inference; monetisation, deployment, and production infrastructure matter too. • 📊🔍 Evals, tracing, and observability are becoming critical for improving reliable agent behaviour in production. posts.text:
Brought MyKo into this world during the 65labs x AI Engineer Hackathon this weekend. MyKo is a desktop presence — a small black cat who lives on your screen, watches what you're doing, and occasionally shares her snarky thoughts about it. 📸 That's her in the screenshot — sitting on the side of the desktop, reading a Kubernetes architecture PDF, and concluding there's nothing to summarize. The architecture: → Gemini Vision reads the screen every 30 seconds and returns a one-sentence description of what's happening → GPT-5.5 receives that description alongside session memory and decides whether MyKo has anything to say → Change detection compares each screenshot against the last — if nothing has changed, the API call is skipped entirely → Document awareness is page-scoped: when a document is open, Gemini reads the visible page — what the user is actively looking at — rather than ingesting the full file. MyKo's awareness is naturally bounded by the user's own attention. → Observations persist across sessions in a local memory file, giving her context that accumulates over time. You can find MyKo napping here : https://lnkd.in/gti4tkyH --- Thank you to my teammates Sardor Madaminov and Amelia Low - it was genuinely easy to work with both of you, and I'm glad we found each other at the venue. A huge thank you to the hosts Sherry Jiang, 🥃 Agrim Singh, Adlin Zainal, Nehal Agrawal, Brian C., Daren T., and sponsors for putting this together. posts.text: AI Engineer Singapore is officially sold out. ten days before we start. this conference is our love letter to the singapore tech scene. for years, we have felt that singapore deserved better AI events. the appetite was always here. the people were always here. but singapore kept getting treated like a place for regional marketing, sales, and business roles, not a place where serious builders live. that never felt right to me. when i first found the scene in 2013, it was alive. meetups every week. hackathons all the time. startup open houses where you could just show up and meet people building things. i still remember meeting someone from RedMart on a friday evening, just after they had raised their first $400k. hackerspace was around. older builders were running events constantly. if you were young and curious, there was a lot to learn from. then, slowly, it faded. i still do not really know when or why. by the time AI arrived, the scene felt different. too much of the oxygen went to people who wanted to be seen talking about AI, not people who were actually making things with it. that was not the scene I fell in love with. for the last two years, my crew and i with 65labs have been trying to bring some of that back. we were teaching people to code with AI in 2024, when half the room had not heard of claude. we ran meetups and hackathons under 65Labs. the biggest cursor hackathon in the region. we ran and supported hackathons for DeepMind and OpenAI. mostly, we just kept showing up and doing the reps. AI Engineer Singapore is what all of that was building toward. and it's not just the 3 days. the leadup has turned into a full singapore summer of AI - we're hosting quality meetups, workshops, hackathons, demo nights all over the city with some of the best companies and our dearest friends. full lineup at www.aievents.sg. this is the first conference in the region built around actually getting your hands dirty. every ticket includes a full day of workshops, because there is no point talking about AI if you are not using it. the rest of the program has the same taste: practical, direct, and built for people who ship. no thought leadership theatre. no "future of AI" panels from people who have not built anything. no roadshow energy. builders talking to builders about what actually works. selling out ten days early feels good. of course it does. but mostly, it makes the hunger impossible to ignore. singapore wants this. maybe it always did. and it is a reminder to us too: this community deserves better than the events it usually gets. to everyone who trusted a first-time conference in Singapore enough to buy a ticket, thank you. genuinely. you took a bet on us before we had proven anything. we will make it count. see you on may 15. Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Adlin Zainal Kaspar Hidayat Ivan Leo Gabriel Chua Congrats team AI Engineer Sg, for pulling off an event of this scale for AI in this region! I would look up to you all AI builder champs to be in Batam in August and build some useful stuff there too. Batam Innovation Center needs all the support to bridge the two regions Absolutely brilliant seeing engineering on center stage again … well done Agrim :) So proud of y’all Sweet stuff! And totally looking forward to geek out for the weekend! Legends, bringing power to the people! Best organisers in Singapore. Absolutely cracked team so sick man! Congrats team!!

posts.text: Thank you, Gabriel! Last week, I won the “Feel the AGI” award at the Codex OpenAI Hackathon. Built in under 4 hours, so definitely a prototype. But the idea was simple and useful: Why should comparing cab fares in Singapore still be manual? For the same ride, prices across 7 taxi / ride-hailing aggregators can differ by SGD 1 to SGD 25, depending on the time of the day and driver load. But opening every app, entering pickup and drop-off, waiting for quotes, and comparing options is tedious. So most people don’t. A consumer should just get the best price. I used Codex to build a cab fare comparison agent. The interesting part was not "Can AI click mobile buttons correctly?" but deciding what should be automated and what should be reasoned through. Pure automation is fast, but brittle. One ad, search suggestion, inconsistent app flows, keyboard, or layout change can break the flow. Pure GenAI is flexible, but using a model for every tap is slow, expensive, and unnecessarily nondeterministic. So I built a hybrid loop. Automation moves quickly through known app flows. GenAI steps in only when interpretation is needed: reading the screen, dismissing overlays, choosing the right field, resolving location suggestions, or deciding the next action. The intent-classification layer kept the task bounded: select pickup, select destination, retrieve fare. No “AI wandering around the phone.” Just constrained execution, visual checkpoints, and recovery when the UI got messy. Latency also needed different kind of framing- for this task, the user doesn't necessarily want to see through every tap happen live rather the result should be completed in background- which shifts the priority to accuracy, auditability, and recoverability at first. The demo had almost no UI by design- just wanted to make the execution loop finer, not build another dashboard. Small Singapore use case. Bigger pattern for consumer automation. posts.text: Singapore Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan built NanoClaw — a self-hosted Claude AI second brain running on Raspberry Pi, with persistent memory and WhatsApp/Telegram integration. Open source. At the CNBC Converge Live fireside chat on April 22, 2026 — the day after publishing NanoClaw — Balakrishnan discussed Singapore's balance between the US and China, the Hormuz crisis supply chain impact, and explicitly framed AI as a strategic diplomatic tool. The timing of the NanoClaw publication alongside his public appearances was deliberate: he was demonstrating, not just describing. His quote from the GitHub gist: "The diplomat who learns to work with AI will have a meaningful edge." What NanoClaw Actually Is NanoClaw is a personal AI agent built from open-source components and documented for replication. The core stack: Base model: Anthropic Claude via API. Balakrishnan chose Claude specifically — the gist documentation notes Claude's reasoning quality and instruction-following as the reasons. The assistant name "NanoClaw" is a direct reference to the underlying model (Claw = Claude). Hardware: Raspberry Pi. Self-hosted, not cloud-dependent. The Pi runs the orchestration layer — managing memory, routing messages, scheduling tasks, and calling the Claude API. Compute-intensive inference still goes to Anthropic's servers via API; the Pi handles everything else locally. Messaging integrations: WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord. The assistant is accessible via any of these channels — you message it as you would message a person. It processes both text and voice notes (voice is transcribed before being passed to Claude), and can handle images. The multimodal input means a diplomat can photograph a document, ask a question about it, and receive analysis instantly. Persistent memory system: The critical architectural piece. Standard LLM conversations are stateless — the model forgets everything between sessions. NanoClaw implements a structured memory layer: facts, context, policy positions, historical precedents, and prior conversations are stored and retrieved to give Claude session-to-session continuity. For a diplomat where institutional knowledge accumulates over years, this compounding memory is what makes the system genuinely useful rather than a novelty. Scheduled tasks: The assistant runs recurring tasks on a schedule — daily briefings compiled from specified sources, reminders, summaries of ongoing negotiations or policy tracks. Set once, runs continuously. Security hardening: Hardened deployments isolate NanoClaw within Docker or Apple Containers, preventing the agent from accessing the host operating system. This is the security boundary that makes running an AI assistant with access to sensitive context tolerable from an infosec perspective. https://lnkd.in/gYp5eefV # Singapore FM Dr Vivian Balakrishnan's AI Assistant NanoClaw

posts.text: A recent article about Singapore’s Foreign Minister, Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan, and his custom “second brain” for diplomacy has been circulating among my peers. It’s a fascinating look at how a leader can delegate cognitive load to a trusted digital system. Progressive and interesting work. You can read the article here. https://lnkd.in/gUpS3WB4 It also highlights a critical distinction that many are missing. A “second brain” is a passive extension of your own mind. The AI agents that businesses are rushing to deploy are intended to be active extensions of your will. And that changes the security conversation entirely. This is the gap I see in nearly every AI strategy session I sit in on across the region. We are building active agents on a passive trust model. The result is a new, subtle form of risk that boils down to three core problems: 1. The "Trusted Servant" Illusion We think of the agent as a trusted servant, like the "second brain." But the moment it acts sending an email, updating a record it stops being a passive library and becomes an active participant in your business processes. Its actions have consequences, but its authority is often dangerously implicit. 2. The "Delegation Black Hole" The "second brain" works because the delegation is simple: it holds your data for you. But how do you delegate authority for an agent to act across three different systems on your behalf? Most setups can't do this securely, creating a black hole where accountability and audibility simply disappear. 3. The Lack of an Actionable Mandate The agent is given a task, but it has no clear, persistent "mandate" that travels with it. It might be verified at the start, but that authority erodes as it moves through a complex workflow. This leaves the agent operating on assumptions a risk no leader should be comfortable with. We can't build a future of automation on a foundation of implied trust. It has to be explicit. That’s why my team and I have consolidated our observations into a simple, non-technical blueprint for how leaders can securely adopt AI. It's not a product pitch. It's a strategic framework for moving from the passive "second brain" model to an active, secure, and governable "second pair of hands." Happy to discuss it with any other leader navigating this challenge. The link is in the comments. Thanks for sharing, Dan. The collision of words... Foreign Minister and nanoclaw don't usually end up in the same sentence. I personally used Notion as my second brain for years. What I've watched happen over time isn't necessarily the replacement, but more of an evolution.. into an LLM context layer that's persistent and structured. posts.text: Fascinating: Singapore’s Foreign Minister just published his personal AI architecture. He’s running his AI second brain on a Raspberry Pi, while most CEOs are still asking ChatGPT to summarize PDFs 😳 Vivian Balakrishnan shared the full setup behind NanoClaw, his self-hosted AI assistant for diplomatic work. It sits on a Raspberry Pi 5 and connects his notes, speeches, briefings, voice memos, research, and messaging workflows into a persistent memory system. Most people still use AI like a vending machine: Ask question. Get answer. Forget everything. Repeat tomorrow. Balakrishnan is using it like infrastructure 🧠 A system that remembers. Synthesizes. Recalls context. Compounds over time. The stack is surprisingly practical: → Raspberry Pi 5 for local hosting → NanoClaw for agent orchestration → Obsidian for human-readable knowledge → SQLite knowledge graph for structured memory → Local embeddings through Ollama → whisper for on-device voice transcription → Docker containers for isolation → Claude Code to assemble the whole thing The key thing here is that he did not build this by becoming a full-time software engineer. He described it as “tool assembly.” And that may be the new executive skill. ↳ Not writing every line of code. ↳ Not outsourcing every workflow to vendors. ↳ But knowing what to combine, what to keep private, and how to make your knowledge system improve every week. This is where AI at work is heading. → From chatbots to second brains. → From prompts to workflows. → From software subscriptions to personal infrastructure. My takeaway here is this: The next productivity gap will not be between people who use AI and people who don’t. It will be between people using rented intelligence and people building owned memory. Because when everyone has access to the same models, the real moat is the context & the data only you control. P.S. check out how I Turned Claude Cowork Into My Personal COO that does work while I sleep 🧠: https://lnkd.in/eS6JCk2G More like a second faulty brain. This setup is fundamentally broken, but for a completely different reason. The fatal flaw is that it relies entirely on Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern. Yes the local hardware might function, however the memory architecture itself is a recipe for silent data corruption. The system works by allowing an AI to constantly rewrite and summarise mutable markdown files in the background. This removes the human completely from the verification loop. If the model hallucinates a single detail during a routine background update, that hallucination permanently overwrites the previous knowledge. Because there is no human curation and no strict audit trail for these changes, small hallucinations will inevitably compound over time. The system will eventually poison its own memory pool, making it far too unreliable for serious executive or diplomatic work. Thx Feels like the real shift isn’t just from tools to infrastructure but from answers to memory that actually shapes decisions. A system can store everything but if it doesn’t change how decisions get made day to day, it’s still just a better archive. Curious where you see that boundary when memory starts becoming leverage, not just storage. The "rented intelligence vs owned memory" framing is good, but it stops short of the real question. A self-hosted Claude assistant with no operator controls, handling diplomatic work, running 24/7 -- that's not just a productivity tool. That's a governance gap waiting to close at the worst possible moment. Tool assembly is the new executive skill. Runtime accountability is the one nobody's talking about yet. the owned memory vs rented intelligence line nails it, doesn’t it? once everyone has the same models, the edge is the context only you as a user can control. that could be the real moat in the end... same shift is hitting finance teams. those that own their data will run circles around teams just renting capability through saas. Do you favour the Karpathy wiki brain or the Nate Jones Open brain approach? Personally I think they are different use cases. open Brain is day to day operational stuff, the wiki is more for research and data analysis. The Raspberry Pi setup is impressive, but I see the contrast with CEOs a bit differently. The barrier for most leaders is not technical skill, it's operational cost. A self-hosted system requires maintenance, security hardening, and a time investment that is hard to justify. The simple PDF summary tool often wins because it has zero operational drag. The more universal the models become, the more personal the advantage becomes. When everyone has access to the same intelligence, the edge shifts to the context only you control. Let's wait for the first AI diplomatic accident: "Sorry, that was a hallucination; we did not declare war on your country, it was my bot's error."

posts.text: When I sat down 3 months ago to build NanoClaw as a personal tool to help me run my company's sales pipeline, I never imagined a foreign minister would use it to help him do international diplomacy at the highest level 🤯 Singapore's Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan shared a detailed technical writeup over the weekend of the personal AI system he built on NanoClaw and runs on a Raspberry Pi. It connects to his WhatsApp and Gmail, transcribes voice notes locally, ingests speeches and articles, and builds up a knowledge graph over time. He says he doesn't dare switch it off. He composed four open-source pieces: NanoClaw, mnemon, OneCLI, and Andrej Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern. He composed existing tools but created something that is uniquely his. What struck me most wasn't what he built. It's what he did next. He didn't keep it internal. He didn't treat it as Singapore's edge. He wrote it up and put it on GitHub. His words: "The diplomat who learns to work with AI will have a meaningful edge. I think that edge is now." When I said as much publicly, he responded with something that's stuck with me: he called what he did "tool assembly." Not coding. Not building from scratch. Assembling the right tools into a system that works for his domain. That's what NanoClaw itself is at its core. Just composition of open-source tools. The thesis is that the assembly is the valuable act, not the individual pieces. There are tens of thousands of professionals building setups like this right now. Doctors, lawyers, researchers, investors. The impulse will be to sit on it. Resist that impulse. By publishing, you become a beacon. Other people working on the same things find you. They share what they're building, suggest improvements, point at things you didn't know existed. You learn faster. You stay in the center of where things are happening. Publishing isn't giving away your edge. It's doubling down on it. This is what real leadership looks like. Taking the initiative to wire up these tools directly into everyday apps and open-sourcing the process shows that the best way to understand the technology is to build it yourself. Amazing hands-on work. It's official - NanoClaw is legit! Wow! We can learn a lot from Singapore The beacon point lands hard - publishing pulls others in, and you learn faster. Worth adding: that same logic applies to governance. As more leaders build assemblies they "don't dare switch off," we'll need to learn from each other on where the final call must remain human. Collectively, that's how we make this a safer space to build in. No one builds from zero. We've always relied on layers: libraries, frameworks, supply chains. Car makers don't make their own tyres. What's changed is the speed of assembly, and how much one person can build and run before needing a team to scale it. Even if you're Singapore's Foreign Minister. Not an ordinary foreign minister, apparently.in case you are not aware of - he was a leading eye doctor (ophthalmologist) before joining politics. Baffling at first, after the immense respect on the work and time invested Gavriel, I'm trying to parse the decision of Vivian made to go public with this, very interesting take because as we both know, retrieval is an unsolved deterministic outcome. posts.text: I spent 7 hours building a visual novel where the NPC is genuinely thinking. There are no dialogue options. You just type what you say to her. You arrive in a dying town. One person knows the safe route through the mountain pass. She doesn't share it with strangers. She notices when you contradict yourself. She warms up slowly, if at all — and some people never get the map. What surprised me most was watching people play it. There's a moment when Mara references something you said three turns ago, or goes quiet in a way that feels loaded, and players just... stop. They start choosing their words more carefully. They start wondering what she actually thinks of them. That's the thing I was chasing. Not a smarter chatbot in a game, but an interaction where the other person feels real enough that you care how it goes, and which changes the direction of the narrative. The stack: GPT-4o by OpenAI for Mara's dialogue, ElevenLabs for her voice (generated live each turn, mood-aware), Lyria powered by Google Gemini for the game's music that shifts as the conversation does, and Ren'Py as the game engine — with the backend deployed on Vercel. The Last Cartographer is on itch.io if you want to try it out. Fair warning — she's not easy to win over. https://lnkd.in/gWPvWSPZ Password in the comments! Demo video: https://lnkd.in/geV2qCdW Built solo at AI Engineer Hackathon Singapore this weekend — thanks to Sherry Jiang, 🥃 Agrim Singh from 65labs, and the organising team for putting it together, and to the sponsors whose credits made it possible: OpenAI, ElevenLabs, Cursor, and Vercel, along with the other numerous companies who made it happen! posts.text: Fires have been making headlines in Singapore with worrying regularity. For most of us, an alarm means grabbing our things and walking out. For an elderly resident, a person with a disability, or someone recovering from illness — that walk may not be possible. And in any one block, it's rarely just one neighbour who could use a hand. SCDF will always be the professionals. But in those first critical minutes before help arrives, the people best placed to act are often already inside the building — fellow residents, a few floors away. That's why I'm spending tomorrow at the AI Engineer Hackathon Singapore building Fire Kaki — a community safety network where a vulnerable resident's SOS reaches on-duty volunteer neighbours within a 2 km radius, instantly. ("Kaki" because help should come from the people next door, not strangers a city away.) The prototype display the core flow: SOS, dispatch, four-role permissions, audit trail. See it in action: https://lnkd.in/gAZemG3h I'm looking for like-minded builders to take it further with me tomorrow. Winning a prize would be a bonus; what I really want is to leave the venue with something that could one day help a real auntie or uncle in our own neighbourhood — or a few of them at once, when minutes matter most. Huge thanks to 65labs, Sherry Jiang, Agrim Singh, and Adlin Zainal for hosting and for the relentless work behind the scenes. #AIEngineer #Hackathon #Singapore #TechForGood #BuildInPublic #AIforGood

posts.text: Fires killed 5 people in Singapore last year — up from 3 the year before. Many were seniors, alone at home. For most of us, an alarm means grabbing our things and walking out. For an elderly resident, a person with a disability, or someone recovering from illness — that walk may not be possible. And in any one block, it's rarely just one neighbour who could use a hand. SCDF will always be the professionals. But in those first critical minutes before help arrives, the people best placed to act are often already inside the building — fellow residents, a few floors away. Jalan Besar GRC saw this and acted. Their Fire Safety Kakis programme trains neighbours to help evacuate vulnerable residents before SCDF arrives — and the model works. What's missing is a platform: most rosters today live on paper or in chat groups, without verification, GPS targeting, or an audit trail. posts.text: Got 15 minutes yesterday with the founder whose AI framework Singapore's Foreign Minister uses as his second brain. Gavriel Cohen is the creator of NanoClaw. For a minister to go on stage and say, I use NanoClaw because it's secure by default and feel free to hack my system, that's bold. Then Gavriel's talk followed and he articulated well how their NanoClaw agent factory speeds up code review with human-in-the-loop approvals. I had to pick his real brain. Three things I walked away with. 1️⃣ When the headlines for an agent are blaring security alerts, CISOs are not going to stick their neck out to adopt them. You need to give assurance that the agent has zero risk of doing something badly. NanoClaw's stance is "don't give agents the ability" in the first place. While I agree in principle, this is going to take real work to constrain the tools they have access to. 2️⃣ Design for distribution. Even in the agentic AI era, this hasn't changed. Pick a vertical you already have a wedge into and get your first customers from there. Not the vertical you find most interesting. The one where you already have the relationships, the credibility, or the lived experience to walk in warm. 3️⃣ Local models for memory compaction may not be reliable enough yet. Compressing context with a small model risks losing the load-bearing detail and distorting what the agent acts on later. For an enterprise that needs everything to run on-premise, that compromise may still be necessary. A quick session, but speaking with a founder who's gotten global traction gave me real insight into how AI leaders are thinking about these problems. Gavriel was very gracious to make his agentic calendar public. I hope in Singapore we get to connect with more founders and speakers this way to learn from the best. I find Gavriel Cohen's insights on NanoClaw's secure-by-default approach crucial for AI adoption. Prioritizing robust security and strategic vertical distribution is paramount for transformative technology to achieve scalable impact, driving industry innovation. Michael Hart any insights/lessons learnt on credential handling, especially on progressive scoping and MCP related? Strong insights from a proven operator. Security-first agent design and vertical wedge distribution are exactly how enterprise AI adoption happens. Systems thinking always beats feature excitement.

posts.text: A country's foreign minister builds an AI second brain to handle diplomatic complexity Here's what almost nobody noticed: this system is a personal knowledge graph. It just isn't called that. The story: Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore's Minister for Foreign Affairs, published the full architecture of his personal AI assistant this weekend. It runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 under his physical control. It ingests his WhatsApp, Gmail, and voice notes. It extracts discrete facts into a graph database - Mnemon, a graph-native memory backend - and synthesises them into structured wiki pages. Semantic recall runs on every query. The system doesn't just retrieve; it builds context over time. The stack: \* NanoClaw (agent orchestration by Gavriel Cohen and Lazer Cohen - amazing story and top of my list) \* Mnemon (knowledge graph memory) \* OneCLI (credential proxy), and the LLM Wiki pattern. All open-source. Sovereignty by design. The killer line from Balakrishnan: he doesn't dare switch it off. When a serving diplomat's personal AI becomes load-bearing infrastructure, the architectural choices start to matter. The bit I want to zoom in on: this is a de facto personal knowledge graph. In 2023, Ivo Velitchkov and I published Personal Knowledge Graphs, the first book on the topic. We argued that a new generation of tools - not necessarily built on traditional KG approaches - was converging toward something deeply familiar: individuals building connected knowledge structures, edge by edge, link by link, over years. Three years later, that convergence is accelerating. Mnemon. Mem0's graph memory layer. cognee. And an ever-rising tide of graph memory backends. Some are lightweight, embeddable, personal-scale graph databases designed for agent state. PKGs in everything but name. And the people adopting them don't even need to know the term knowledge graph to benefit. Others aim at enterprises. But this goes beyond the standard definition of knowledge graphs, in which "enterprise" was everything but spelled out. For close to a decade I've been tracking all things graph. This emerging Graph + AI / Agent Memory frontier is the fastest moving edge I've seen. Nobody has fully mapped it yet. That's what we're building at State of the Graph: https://lnkd.in/dVpyC4EC The Personal Knowledge Graph Book called this: https://lnkd.in/dMJ7tjEE Have you used a personal knowledge graph without calling it that? And now that a foreign minister trusts one, does that change how seriously you take the pattern? → Graph vendor trying to stand out in this fast-moving space? I help tech companies build visibility before the category gets crowded. → Technologist evaluating graph memory backends or building your own agent stack, and you want a map of the landscape before you commit? Let's compare notes. → Investor or analyst looking to chart this market and spot the next breakout? DM me. Great! (though I'm not a fan of the image) Impressive capability—but this is exactly where structure matters. What’s being shown is a powerful Performer (AI) executing full activity chains. The risk isn’t failure—it’s authority drift and expertise erosion. Transparency and inspectability help, but they’re not enough. Visibility ≠ governance. What’s missing is: -Explicit human authority over lifecycle stages -Controlled decision context and definitions -Persistent knowledge capture from each run Without that, humans shift from decision-makers to observers—and capability atrophies. The opportunity is bigger than “AI that works fast.” It’s AI whose every action becomes governed, traceable, and reusable knowledge—so capability compounds instead of disappearing. That’s the difference between automation… and sustainable intelligence. Ellie Rofe thats interesting case to check it out Great analysis my friend! State of the Graph look very cool.

posts.text:
I wasn't expecting a Minister for Foreign Affairs to share his AI insights at a Tech event.🤯

When you think of a Minister for Foreign Affairs, you probably don't picture someone running a personalized AI agent off an old Raspberry Pi. But Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan's recent keynote is full of surprises. Before his long career in politics, he was an eye surgeon, and he remains an avid tinkerer who assembles watches and reprograms appliances in his spare time.

His perspective on AI is incredibly grounded and practical. Here is a quick takeaway of his core points on adopting AI tools:
- ​Tool Assembly over Coding: You don't necessarily need to write complex code to build something useful; you can assemble existing open-source tools (like Nano Claw, Ollama, and Obsidian) to turbocharge your own productivity
- Learn by Doing: You cannot effectively govern or utilize a technology you have only been briefed on. You have to get your hands dirty and experiment with the tools yourself

posts.text: This is why I love having these two gens in my team ❤️ REACHY RAP BATTLE SHOWDOWN - AI.ENGINEER SINGAPORE Unveiled at ai.engineer in Singapore today (Thorsten Schaeff as promised 🤣) Hugging Face Pollen Robotics Reachy rap battle, powered by Google DeepMind, ElevenLabs and more... Along with my long time collaborator Dr Richard Savery we built a real-time AI rap battle system with two Reachy Mini robots. (1) The flow: A human drops a prompt spoken on the mic. Local speech-to-text transcribes the prompt on an Apple Silicon Mac using MLX Whisper. The text is sent to Google DeepMind Gemini, which writes alternating rap battle verses for two characters. Each battle verse is rendered with custom ElevenLabs voices. The system combines the voices into a stereo battle track, with one rapper on the left channel and the other on the right. At the same time, we generate a timing manifest that maps each rap turn to a specific robot animation. Cycling '74 Max/MSP handles playback and show control. Python handles AI generation, voice rendering, timing, OSC messages, and robot choreography. The two Reachy Mini robots connect over WiFi and USB. When the battle plays, each robot performs when its voice is rapping, while the other keeps a smaller beat-driven groove so both stay alive on stage. The robots’ movement is word-aware: emphasized words create stronger gestures, and each robot has its own animation personality. The system prewarms robot connections before playback so audio and motion start in sync. (2) the Stack: Max/MSP, Python, Gemini, ElevenLabs, MLX Whisper, OSC, Reachy Mini SDK, Apple Silicon. A small fun idea turned into a full AI performance pipeline: prompt in, rap battle out, two robots arguing on beat 😎 And as mentioned in the video, special thanks to 🥃 Agrim Singh and Sherry Jiang and the whole 65labs team for making ai.engineer Singapore happen, and for listening to my crazy ideas about setting up a Robot Playground for the Embodied AI track! A few battle highlights in the video!

posts.text: ai engineer singapore just wrapped, and i still don’t think i’ve fully processed it - or recovered from the sleep deprivation. this was a labor of love from our organizing team. i’m still sitting with everything that happened, but i wanted to share a few moments that stayed with me most. speakers flying in from around the world - many of whom we’d only known through the internet - showing up for builders here in singapore. staying late after talks, talking to students, and genuinely wanting to help (some even sharing they're thinking of moving to singapore 👀 ) minister Vivian Balakrishnan showing what it looks like when a world leader doesn’t just get briefed on ai, but actually tinkers with the tools himself. that conversation alone has already sparked debate and reached millions online. students realizing the infrastructure and access are already here - made possible by individual people who chose to sponsor scholars - to show up and care enough to support the next generation. and across almost every session, the same thread kept emerging: ai is forcing us to think more deeply about what it actually means to be human. finally, the closing line hit me hard: “you are the scene.” i moved from silicon valley to singapore in 2018, and this place embraced me. over the past 8 years, i’ve seen how much talent exists here - often in ways that are quietly underestimated. for a long time, it felt heartbreaking to hear people talk about singapore tech as if the only path forward was to leave - for founders to move abroad, for funds to pull out, for ambitious people to believe the real opportunities existed somewhere else. this weekend reminded me how wrong that narrative is. speakers, sponsors, founders, researchers, and engineers flew in from around the world because they believe something important is happening here. the scene is already here - and it was sitting in that room. i see singapore as a forward-deployed nation - a place where frontier technology meets everyday people and companies faster than almost anywhere else in the world. we tell people learning to vibe code that it only takes one step. this weekend felt like a first step toward something much bigger. more reflections soon. for now: grateful, overwhelmed, and already thinking about what comes next. 🥃 Agrim Singh Nehal Agrawal Adlin Zainal Ivan Leo Kaspar Hidayat Brian C. Daren T. 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan

posts.text: One of the most insightful conversations on AI I’ve heard recently came from Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs. Not because it was technical. Because it was deeply practical. Dr. Balakrishnan spoke about using a personalized AI agent — his “second brain” — to manage the cognitive complexity of international diplomacy. -No hype. -No futuristic narrative. Just a leader openly explaining how AI is becoming part of his daily workflow and decision-making process. My Top 3 Learnings from this conversation: 1️⃣ AI adoption becomes real when it becomes personal The biggest shift is not organizations deploying AI platforms. It is individuals redesigning how they think, learn, prepare, and execute using AI in their own workflows. 2️⃣ The barrier to experimentation has collapsed You no longer need to be an engineer to build meaningful AI-enabled systems. Curiosity, iteration, and “learning by doing” are becoming more valuable than waiting for perfect enterprise transformation programs. 3️⃣ AI can augment capability — but not accountability This was perhaps the most important point. AI can synthesize information and accelerate execution, but judgment, context, ethics, and responsibility still remain deeply human. 💡 That balance may define the next generation of leadership.💡 The leaders who experiment personally with AI tools will likely understand this transformation far better than those who only discuss it strategically from a distance. Simple message. Powerful implications for the future of work and leadership. Video: https://lnkd.in/g38ctD8y

posts.text:
The "AI Gold Rush" of simple prompting is officially dead. The era of Contextual Infrastructure has arrived.

Last week at AI Engineer Singapore, the late-night founder dinners, community mixers, and closed-door builder sessions made one thing abundantly clear:

The market has hit absolute fatigue with isolated AI tools and shiny point-solution wrappers. If your AI system can’t connect fragmented data, handle complex multi-step logic, and operate with deterministic accuracy, it’s just noise.

At Insight Genesis (IGAi), these conversations match exactly what AI should be building towards to. The real value in AI has migrated from generating content to correlating data into deep human insights.

Here are the 3 structural shifts every founder, builder, and enterprise operator needs to watch right now:

1. From Isolated Tools to Data Fabrics
Organizations don’t want another chatbot that reads a single PDF. They need systems that sit across completely disconnected silos—multimodal streams like real-time voice, video analytics, and behavioral data—and map out hidden patterns, intent, and decision-making. True utility means moving from an AI that answers questions to a system that predicts behavior.

2. Multi-Agent Systems & MCP Are the Backbone
To build systems that understand human nuance reliably, engineers are abandoning single-model prompts. Production-grade deployment requires specialized multi-agent loops—where an Ingestion Agent filters raw telemetry, an Analytics Agent models behavioral data, and an Auditor Agent checks the output for accuracy.

3. Privacy-First & Decentralized Ownership
For an AI to provide deeply personalized insights, it needs access to highly sensitive data (wellness, biometrics, daily habits). The massive consensus among APAC builders is that privacy-first infrastructure is the ultimate gatekeeper for enterprise rollout. This is driving the convergence of AI + Web3, allowing users to retain sovereignty over their data vectors while training local or edge-based models securely.

My takeaway:
- The barrier to entry for building raw software has collapsed to near zero, which means the value of generic AI tools has dropped to zero alongside it.
-The builders who win the next wave won't be the ones with the best prompt. They will be the ones building sovereign, multi-agent frameworks capable of securely binding fragmented personal data into actionable intelligence.

Huge respect to the organizers, researchers, and builders pushing the boundaries in Singapore. For those building AI in Singapore, we are just getting started. 

My question is this: What is the biggest bottleneck you're facing when moving AI from prototype to production-grade deployment? 

Share them in the comments below. 

#AIEngineer #AgenticWorkflows #InsightGenesis #IGAi #PrivacyFirstAI #Web3 #SingaporeTech

posts.text: Wanted to extend a massive thanks to the 65labs and the AI Engineer team for bringing strong "Builder" energy to Singapore. It was energizing (and occasionally exhausting!) to be surrounded by developers, designers, and fellow tinkerers over the past week. Was nice seeing familiar faces, while also making new connections. Also equally cool running into people you normally hear on your favorite podcasts (like swyx of the Latent Space Podcast - please check it out if you haven't yet). While I'm under no illusions that Singapore is some kind of global AI epicenter, there were still many things I felt proud of. 1. Seeing our Foreign Minister openly share his NanoClaw set-up. I think that takes leadership, particularly in front of a discerning technical audience. AI is also becoming an increasingly politically sensitive topic, so you're bound to become a lightning rod of sorts. 2. Meeting Singaporean founders who are based globally, but still want to contribute locally. 3. Watching a group of people 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 in support of what they believe in, even without broad consensus support (Sherry Jiang Agrim Singh Rachael De Foe Ivan Leo Brian C. Daren T. and many more). Events like this help inspire people (young and old) to build closer to the frontier - even when the landscape looks unclear. In Singapore, we often wait to see what institutions, incumbents, or the broader market validates before deciding what is acceptable to pursue. That approach isn't without merit. It creates some stability and predictability. But it can also make it harder for unconventional folks, creatives, or early builders to experiment at the edges before the rest of society catches up. A lot of what makes Singapore work today came from earlier generations 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝗻-𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘀𝘂𝘀, but eventually proved correct. --- • Building a container terminal before container demand was clear; • Moving the airport from Paya Lebar to Changi in anticipation of the jumbo jet; • Even how we 'exited' ourselves from Malaysia in 1965 [Go visit the excellent Albatross File exhibition at the National Library if you haven't] --- We're living in a world with fewer templates to follow. We need more people willing to make thoughtful, non-consensus bets to build the future. * +6 Good bumping into you! non-consensus bets are the way to go!!
